summary: The shipped `Cursor` type doc says "core never parses, compares, or sorts by cursor value", and the package README repeats it as "core never parses or compares them". `seam.ts` says the opposite and states the requirement that follows ("it does compare two for byte equality, as the no-progress brake in `catchUpTopic`. A cursor naming a position must therefore be byte-stable across calls"), and `engine/catchup.ts:71` is `if (messages.length === 0 || nextCursor === since) return total;`. Two shipped specifications of the same contract disagree, and the false one sits on the type a plugin author imports.
failure: A plugin author reads `dist/message.d.ts`'s `Cursor` doc, concludes byte-stability is not required, and mints a cursor by re-serialising a position (e.g. `JSON.stringify({t, seq})` with non-deterministic key order, or a re-rendered ISO timestamp). Input: a topic drained to its end whose plugin returns a semantically identical but byte-different `nextCursor` per call. Output: `catchUpTopic`'s `nextCursor === since` brake never fires, so catch-up keeps paging an exhausted topic until the page bound trips; the symmetric error stops early and silently drops messages. Nothing in core's suite grades the README sentence or that doc line.
remediation: Make the `Cursor` JSDoc state the real contract — opaque in that core never PARSES or ORDERS it, but does compare two for byte equality as the no-progress brake, so a cursor naming a position must be byte-stable across calls — and change the README's "core never parses or compares them" to match. Add a row to `packages/bridge-core/src/transport/tool-docs-parity.test.ts` (which already reads the core README) that fails when either site asserts opacity without the byte-stability qualifier.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a public doc asserts an absolute about core's treatment of the cursor that the engine violates": a table of (documentation site, claim regex) over `seam.ts`, `message.ts`, `README.md` and `DESIGN.md` §6 asserting every site mentioning cursor opacity also mentions the byte-equality comparison — paired with a behavioural row driving `catchUpTopic` against a plugin whose `nextCursor` is semantically stable but byte-unstable, asserting termination for the documented reason. Existing `engine/catchup.test.ts` rows use byte-stable string cursors and cannot see the divergence.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `engine/catchup.ts:71` — `if (messages.length === 0 || nextCursor === since) return total;` — the only cursor comparison I traced; and `transport/tool-docs-parity.test.ts:26`, which already does `readFileSync(new URL('../../README.md', import.meta.url))`.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — doc text plus a new assertion; no runtime input changes.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A future README/JSDoc edit restoring the absolute "never compares" phrasing would newly fail CI. No runtime input newly rejected.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I grepped for tests reading `bridge-core/README.md` (only `transport/tool-docs-parity.test.ts`, which asserts only the tool table) and for tests asserting the `Cursor` doc text (none). Doc-only edits cannot change `Object.keys(api)`, so `index.test.ts` is unaffected.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing would be fixed by code changes — the code is correct and the doc is wrong, so the doc is the defect. If only the README is corrected and `message.ts` is not, the `.d.ts` a plugin author reads in their editor still carries the false claim.

JSDoc on an interface MEMBER ships verbatim in `.d.ts` and is invisible to it — and a live violation sits behind the hole: `allowlist.ts:48`, in `AllowlistOptions.postPatterns` (a barrel-exported type), says "capped at {@link MAX_POST_TOPICS}", and `index.ts` does not export `MAX_POST_TOPICS`.

Output: the guard reports zero offenders. Separately close the live instance by adding `MAX_POST_TOPICS` to the `./config.js` export clause in `index.ts`, next to `MAX_BLOCK_MS`.

The current `finds documented exports…` row only asserts `documented.length > 20`, which a scanner blind to every member doc still satisfies.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `index.test.ts:100` `EXPORT_DECL` and `:99-131` (the block/owner walk) — the `else` arm clearing `block = null` on any non-continuation line is what discards member docs; and `index.ts:26-37`, the `./config.js` clause that exports `MAX_BLOCK_MS` but not `MAX_POST_TOPICS`.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Any member-level `{@link X}` where X is an exported value the barrel withholds. Concretely it would newly flag `config.ts:73`/`:88` (`{@link MAX_RECORD_TOPICS}`, `{@link MAX_POST_TOPICS}`) if the depth tracker attributes those to `ConfigSchema` — I did NOT trace whether tsc propagates zod object-member JSDoc into `ConfigSchema`'s emitted type, so that pair may be a false positive the fix must exclude.

summary: `commentaryOf` recognises a comment only when the line carries `//`/`/*` after string-blanking, or when the trimmed line starts with `*`. A `/* … */` block whose continuation lines start with anything else is invisible to ALL THREE lints — including the prime-directive prose rule ("in bridge-core, names a backend plugin package"), described in the file as catching the one form of backend dependency the import graph cannot.
failure:
Input: append to `packages/bridge-core/src/mentions.ts`:
/*

*/
That is two simultaneous violations (self-dating prose; bridge-core prose naming a backend plugin package). Output: `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core/src/source-hygiene.test.ts` → 60 passed, 0 failed. The same text written as `//` or as a ` * ` JSDoc continuation is caught.
remediation: Make `commentaryOf` stateful across the file: carry an `inBlockComment` flag set by an unterminated `/*` (after string blanking) and cleared by `*/`, treating every line while set as commentary. Keep the per-line signature for the fixture rows by threading the flag as a parameter defaulting to `false`.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a comment shape the scanner cannot see": parameterise the existing `scans %s` fixture table by COMMENT SHAPE — `//`, trailing `//`, ` * ` JSDoc continuation, `/* one-line */`, a multi-line `/* */` continuation with no leading `*`, and a continuation line containing a quote character — each asserted to classify as commentary and each paired with a code-that-quotes-it row asserted not to. The current five rows are all shapes the scanner already sees, so they cannot distinguish a working scanner from one blind to half the grammar.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `source-hygiene.test.ts:95` `const code = line.replace(STRINGS, …)` (string blanking, which must run before looking for `/*` so a quoted `/*` does not open a phantom block) and `:100` `const block = trimmed.startsWith('*') ? trimmed : ''`, the arm that today handles only JSDoc continuations.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Text inside multi-line `/* */` blocks anywhere under `packages/` and `examples/` becomes lintable, so any existing such block containing `as of now`, a tracker id, or (in bridge-core) `bridge-<backend>` starts failing. I did not enumerate the repo for pre-existing offences in that shape, so the fix may reveal debt.

A `MAX_*`/`MIN_*`/`DEFAULT_*` export added to any other module directly under `src/` is never pinned to a value nor paired with a realistic-input row. CLAUDE.md's standing rule requires a glob over `src/**` rather than named files.
failure: Input: append `export const MAX_ZZZ_LIMIT = 5;` to `packages/bridge-core/src/mentions.ts`. Output: `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core/src/stated-bounds.test.ts` → 41 passed. The new capacity has no pinned literal and no realistic-input row, so it can later be tightened to any value under a green suite — precisely what the file's own header ("grading a bound only through probes DERIVED from it leaves its VALUE free") exists to prevent.
remediation: Replace `CAPACITY_MODULES` with a directory walk over `src/*.ts` (excluding `*.test.ts`), keeping an explicit named exemption list for directories another target owns (`engine/`, `transport/`, `auth/`) — an exemption is visible and reviewable; a whitelist of four filenames is not.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a capacity constant exists with nothing pinning its value": derive the graded set from a glob over the source tree, assert the derived set is non-empty and covers each governed directory, and keep the existing `declared.sort() === CAPACITIES.names.sort()` equality so both an addition and a move fail. The equality already catches a MOVE; only an ADDITION in an unlisted module escapes, so the glob is the whole fix.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `stated-bounds.test.ts:294-302` — `CAPACITY_MODULES.flatMap(…matchAll(/^export const ((?:MAX|MIN|DEFAULT)_[A-Z0-9_]+)\b/gm))` and the `expect(declared.sort()).toEqual(CAPACITIES.map(c => c.name).sort())` that follows.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: An unscoped glob immediately picks up `engine/presence.ts`'s MAX_HANDLE_LEN, MAX_TOPIC_LEN, MAX_RECORD_TOPICS, MAX_INSTANCE_ID_LEN, MAX_HANDLE_INSTANCES, MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS, `engine/presence-reach.ts`'s MAX_PEER_PATTERN_LEN and `transport/tools.ts`'s MAX_FETCH_LIMIT — the equality goes red until each gets a row or an exemption. That is real work crossing into another target's files, so a `src/*.ts`-scoped glob plus named exemptions is the smaller correct move.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: `stated-bounds.test.ts > has a row for every capacity the governed modules export` fails immediately on an unscoped glob. No other test reads `CAPACITY_MODULES`; I grepped and it appears only in this file.

summary: `tsconfig.json` includes `src/**/*` and excludes only `src/**/*.test.ts`, so `src/testing/**` compiles into `dist/testing/**` and ships under `files: ["dist"]`. The `exports` map has only `"."` and `"./package.json"`, so no consumer can import any of it. The tarball carries a fake OIDC IdP that mints RS256-signed JWTs, an in-memory MCP client/server harness, a fake backend plugin and an express fixture — all unreachable. The one in-repo consumer imports it by relative source path (`examples/self-host-remote/test/oidc-smoke.test.ts:7`), calling it "the internal test helper".
failure: Input: `cd packages/bridge-core && npx tsc -b`. Output: `dist/testing/` — 40 files, 164 KB — including `fake-oidc.js`, `tool-harness.js`, `http-app.js`, `fake-plugin.js`. Importing `@sharptrick/parley-core/testing/fake-oidc.js` from a consumer fails with ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED, so the bytes serve no consumer. The existing packaging rule ("ships only what a consumer can run") passes, because it grades only test-named artifacts and undeclared imports, never unreachable ones.
remediation: Either exclude `src/testing/**` from the published build (add it to `tsconfig.json`'s `exclude` beside `src/**/*.test.ts`; `tsconfig.test.json` overrides `exclude: []` so it stays type-checked), or publish it deliberately with an `"./testing/*"` export subpath. Excluding is the smaller move, since the in-repo consumer imports source, not dist.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "the tarball carries a module no export path can reach": add a row to `packaging.test.ts` that, per public workspace, resolves each emitted `dist/**/*.js` against the manifest's `exports` map (wildcards included) and asserts every emitted module is either an exported entry or transitively imported by one — catching the next internal directory that leaks into the build, not just `testing/`.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `packages/bridge-core/tsconfig.json` (`"include": ["src/**/*"], "exclude": ["src/**/*.test.ts"]`), `package.json` `"files": ["dist"]` and the two-entry `exports` map, and `tsconfig.test.json`'s `"exclude": []` which keeps the excluded surface type-checked.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Excluding `src/testing/**` removes `dist/testing/*.d.ts`; any in-repo consumer importing it through the compiled build rather than the vitest source alias would break. I found exactly one importer and it imports `…/src/testing/fake-oidc.js` (source, resolved by the alias). I did NOT check whether sibling `tsc -b` project references pull `dist/testing/*.d.ts` in.

I did not run the full suite after this change.

The failure is the maintenance shape: a reviewer widening the anchoring class widens one table, while the corpus doc asserts — falsely — that widening the single list widens every site.

summary: `hostnameOf` splits on `:` for any value that does not start with `[`, so an unbracketed IPv6 literal in `allowedHosts` reduces to the empty string. The operator's intended host is then never allowed, and `''` joins the allow set, where it matches a request that carries no Host header at all. Both halves of the DNS-rebinding gate move the wrong way from one plausible config value, with no error and no log.
failure: `createRemoteHttpApp(plugin, cfg, { insecureNoAuth: true, allowedHosts: ['::1', 'parley.internal'] })`. Reproduced over a raw socket: `POST /mcp HTTP/1.1` with `Host: [::1]` -> 403 (the operator's own IPv6 loopback client is locked out); `POST /mcp HTTP/1.0` with the Host header omitted -> passes the gate and reaches the MCP transport (400 from downstream), where the identical request against the loopback default returns the gate's 403. `hostnameOf('::1') === ''` and `hostnameOf('') === ''`.
remediation: Normalise and validate `allowedHosts` at construction: parse each entry with `new URL(v.includes('://') ? v : \`http://${v}\`).hostname` (which handles `::1` by requiring brackets and throws on a value that names no host), and throw a RangeError naming the offending entry when the result is empty. Separately, treat a missing/empty `Host` as refused explicitly rather than as a lookup of `''`.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a configured gate value that the parser silently maps to something that matches nothing, or matches too much'. Widen the existing `allowedHosts` table in http-gating.test.ts into a parameterized (configured-entry x incoming-Host) grid whose configured axis includes `::1`, `[::1]`, `[::1]:8443`, `fe80::1%eth0`, `''`, `':8080'` and `'http://parley.example:8443'`, and assert two properties per row rather than one status: (1) every legal entry admits the host it names — so a collapse-to-empty entry fails as a lockout — and (2) the request with NO Host header is refused on EVERY configuration — so no entry can widen the set to the empty string. Add a direct property test over `hostnameOf` asserting the result is non-empty for every entry the constructor accepts.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `new URL()` from node's WHATWG parser: `new URL('http://::1')` throws (Invalid URL) while `new URL('http://[::1]')` yields hostname `[::1]`, and `new URL('http://parley.example:8443').hostname` is `parley.example` — the same lowercasing the current `.toLowerCase()` provides. It also relies on the gate branch `!allowed.has(hostnameOf(req.headers.host ?? ''))` staying a Set membership test.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: nothing on the request path; on the config path it accepts nothing it does not already accept.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: an `allowedHosts` entry that names no host — `'::1'`, `''`, `':8080'` — now throws at `createRemoteHttpApp` instead of being silently kept. A deployment currently running with `allowedHosts: ['::1']` (and being 403'd for it) would fail to start rather than fail to serve.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I grepped every `allowedHosts` call site in packages/bridge-core/src/transport/http-gating.test.ts and packages/bridge-core/src/testing/http-app.ts: the values used are `['parley.internal']`, `['Parley.Internal','HTTPS://Parley.Example:8443']`, `['parley.example.com']` and the LOOPBACK_HOSTS default `['127.0.0.1','localhost','[::1]']`, all of which parse to a non-empty hostname. I did not grep the auth/ suites' RemoteHttpOptions usage.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the bug remained, nothing: the fix is at the config boundary and the parser bug is what it detects. If only the empty-string half were closed (reject `''` from the allow set) the lockout half would remain — a bare-IPv6 operator would still get 403 on every legitimate request, now permanently.

summary: `peerReach` truncates the match input to MAX_MATCH_INPUT (64) and matches the peer's anchored pattern against the PREFIX, while `Allowlist.has` refuses an over-64 input outright. Config permits a topic name up to MAX_TOPIC_LEN (512), so the two sites of the same 'anchor an untrusted source' rule return opposite verdicts for a perfectly legal deployment, and `parley_list_users` reports peers as reachable on a topic they cannot post to. The comment justifying the clamp ('our topic names are short') is false against the schema the loader accepts.
failure: Config `topics: ['ops-' + 'x'.repeat(70)]` (74 chars, accepted by ConfigSchema). A peer beats `postTopics: ['.{64}']`. `new RegExp('^(?:.{64})$').test(myTopic)` is false — the peer genuinely cannot post there — yet `filterReachable([peer], { canPostTo, mySubscribedTopics: [myTopic] })` returns the peer. Reproduced for the scoped path too, and for sources `.*`, `ops-.*` and `[a-z0-9-]+` against a 100-char topic, where `Allowlist.has` answers false and both `filterReachable` shapes answer true. The agent hands off to a peer that will never receive the message.
remediation: Make the two sites answer identically by refusing rather than truncating: in `peerReach`, `if (input.length > MAX_MATCH_INPUT) return false;` instead of slicing — matching `Allowlist.has`'s `if (topic.length > MAX_MATCH_INPUT) return false`. Then close the gap that makes the regime reachable at all: cap `topics` and `post_topics` entries in ConfigSchema at MAX_MATCH_INPUT rather than MAX_TOPIC_LEN, so a topic core cannot pattern-match is refused at load with a message saying so.
testUpgrade: The class is 'one rule, two implementations, graded only inside the region where they happen to agree'. The corpus in packages/bridge-core/src/testing/anchoring-corpus.ts is the right shape but every input is under 64 chars, so the length axis is invisible. Add an explicit input-LENGTH axis to it — each row replayed at |input| = 1, MAX_MATCH_INPUT - 1, MAX_MATCH_INPUT, MAX_MATCH_INPUT + 1 and MAX_TOPIC_LEN — and keep anchoring-parity.test.ts's rule that all registered sites must return the SAME verdict per cell. That makes any future clamp/refuse divergence a failure at the boundary rather than a behaviour nobody sampled. Also widen the CPU-budget table's `callerReach`, which currently pads every caller topic to exactly MAX_MATCH_INPUT and so never leaves the agreeing region.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `Allowlist.has`'s existing branch `if (topic.length > MAX_MATCH_INPUT) return false;` as the reference semantics, and on `filterReachable`'s scoped arm `e.topics.includes(opts.scope) || reaches(...)` — the explicit-subscription arm is untouched, so a peer that LISTS the long topic still surfaces.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: a peer whose pattern matches only the 64-char prefix of an over-long topic is no longer reported reachable. If the config half is also applied, a config with a topic longer than 64 chars is refused at load — a deployment running one today would fail to start.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: packages/bridge-core/src/engine/presence.test.ts > 'a screened pattern stays cheap however long the matched topic is' > 'still matches on the bounded prefix of an over-long topic' asserts exactly the behaviour I am removing; it must be rewritten to assert refusal. I did not run the mutation, so I have not enumerated collateral failures in list-users-tool.test.ts or the conformance suite.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixing only presence-reach removes the false positive but leaves the reverse asymmetry: a legitimately-configured 100-char topic remains unmatchable by any post pattern anywhere, silently, which is why the config cap is the other half. Fixing only the config cap leaves the clamp in place for any embedder that builds an Allowlist by hand.

summary: `parley_fetch_recent` clamps the requested `limit` but never bounds the page it hands back, even though MAX_FETCH_LIMIT's own JSDoc names the result-side consequence ('core then walks the whole result twice... an unbounded page is a denial-of-service knob'). The seam explicitly permits over-delivery — packages/bridge-core/src/testing/nonconformant.ts ships 'a page LONGER than the requested limit' as a shape core must survive — and `parley_list_users` guards it with `slice(-PRESENCE_FETCH_LIMIT)`, so the same risk is handled at one tool and trusted at the other. With `limit` omitted there is no bound at all.
failure: A plugin whose `fetchRecent` returns 5000 messages. Driven through the real MCP client with `{ topic: 'ctx', limit: 1 }`: the tool result carries all 5000 messages / 1,071,716 bytes of text into the agent's context, and the warm-up loop `for (const m of result.messages) deps.seen?.markSeen(...)` writes 5000 ids into a 4096-entry FIFO — `seen.has('ctx', '0')` is false afterwards, so the topic's dedup window has been flushed and the push loop can re-emit messages the agent already pulled.
remediation: Bound the page in the handler: `const cap = Math.min(args.limit ?? MAX_FETCH_LIMIT, MAX_FETCH_LIMIT); const kept = result.messages.length > cap ? result.messages.slice(0, cap) : result.messages; const nextCursor = kept.length < result.messages.length ? kept.at(-1)!.cursor : result.nextCursor;` then warm `seen` from `kept` and return `{ messages: kept, nextCursor }`. Taking the HEAD and re-deriving nextCursor from the last retained message keeps the cursor pointing at what was actually delivered, so the caller pages the remainder instead of losing it.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a seam result core forwards without applying the bound it applied to the request'. Parameterize a table over (tool, seam method, over-delivering shape) driving every result-returning tool — parley_fetch_recent today, list_users already covered — from NONCONFORMANT_SHAPES rather than from a hand-written plugin, and assert three invariants per cell: the returned page is <= the effective cap, the returned nextCursor equals the cursor of the last returned message, and the dedup window still contains the FIRST id of the page (which is what catches the seen-set flush). Widen NONCONFORMANT_SHAPES' over-delivery factor from `limit + 5` to a multiple that exceeds MAX_FETCH_LIMIT and SEEN_MAX_PER_TOPIC, so the shape can reach the caps it is meant to probe.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: DESIGN 6's plugin ordering guarantee (messages ascending by cursor), so that `kept.at(-1)!.cursor` is the greatest cursor delivered and the derived nextCursor is monotone; and on `Message.cursor` being present on every message, which message.ts's type requires.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: nothing is rejected; an over-delivering plugin's surplus is now truncated rather than forwarded. A caller that today receives 5000 messages in one page now receives 1000 plus a cursor that reaches the rest.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none — I applied this exact edit and ran the whole bridge-core suite: 50 files / 2832 tests passed unmodified, then reverted. I did NOT run packages/conformance against the backends, so a plugin suite that asserts the tool echoes its page verbatim would not have been seen.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the truncation were applied but nextCursor were left as the plugin's, the surplus messages would be skipped forever — strictly worse than the DoS, which is why re-deriving the cursor is load-bearing rather than cosmetic. Applied as written with the bug otherwise unaddressed, the remaining exposure is the serialisation cost of assembling the 5000-message page inside the plugin before core sees it.

summary: `classifyDbError` classifies by error `code` OR by message text. The `node:sqlite` fallback driver — which this package ships, declares in `engines`, and grades everywhere else — stamps `code: 'ERR_SQLITE_ERROR'` on EVERY error class, so the message arms are the only thing that classifies anything on that driver. No test in the package ever exercises them: the 9-row `ERROR_CASES` matrix in background-jobs.test.ts and the `IOERR/CORRUPT/BUSY` helpers in subscription-health.test.ts fabricate better-sqlite3-shaped errors (`{code:'SQLITE_BUSY'}`), a shape node:sqlite never produces, and driver-parity.test.ts grades pragmas, at-rest mode, RunResult shape and a seam round-trip but not classification.
failure: Mutation applied and verified: delete `|| /database is locked|database table is locked/i.test(msg)` from the lock arm and `malformed|file is not a database` from the fatal arm, leaving code-only matching. All 597 tests in `packages/bridge-sqlite` stay green, including `conformance.test.ts` run twice (once per driver) and all of driver-parity. Probe (`node` + real drivers) confirms node:sqlite reports a locked write as `{code:'ERR_SQLITE_ERROR', errstr:'…'}` and a corrupt file as `{code:'ERR_SQLITE_ERROR', message:'file is not a database'}`. Under that mutation, on a node:sqlite install: every WAL contention tick classifies as `unavailable` → a stderr line per topic per minute (README: lock is "the one class not worth reporting"), and 10 consecutive contended ticks escalate the topic to `degraded` with a backoff to 30 s — live push throttled by nothing but normal peer writes.

In `test/driver-parity.test.ts`, for each `kind`, provoke REAL errors and assert `classifyDbError(caught)`: (a) lock — fork `test/lock-holder.mjs`, open with `openDriver(path, { busyTimeoutMs: 0 })`, attempt an insert; (b) fatal — `openDriver` a file written with non-database bytes; (c) unavailable — a statement against a path made read-only. Separately, parameterize background-jobs' `ERROR_CASES` over an `errorShape` axis so each row is also built in node:sqlite's shape (`{ code: 'ERR_SQLITE_ERROR', errcode, errstr, message }`).

Concretely, a `describe.each(KINDS)` block asserting `classifyDbError` on errors produced BY that driver (never hand-built), plus an `errorShape` axis on background-jobs' `ERROR_CASES` so the synthetic rows cover both `code` conventions. The existing rows are too narrow because each supplies the code its own arm matches, so both arms of the `||` can never be graded independently.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `openDriver(path, opts)`'s existing `busyTimeoutMs` option (driver.ts:105 `opts.busyTimeoutMs ?? 5000`) and `test/lock-holder.mjs`, both already used by test/multi-process.test.ts's "a configured timeout retries for its full window" case; and `classifyDbError` itself, unchanged.

summary: `backoffMs` is `Math.min(pollIntervalMs * 2 ** doublings, 30_000)`. For any `poll_interval_ms` above the 30 s ceiling the function returns LESS than the configured interval, so escalation makes the loop poll a store that is already failing MORE often than when it was healthy. `poll_interval_ms` is validated up to 2 147 483 647 ms and the README calls it "a pure latency/cost knob", so this is reachable from a documented, endorsed configuration.
failure: `poll_interval_ms: 60000` (valid; accepted by `validateBackendConfig`). Store becomes unreachable → after 10 consecutive failures `health.state='degraded'` and `delay = backoffMs(60000, 10) = min(120000, 30000) = 30000`. The loop now issues a `selectAfter` every 30 s instead of every 60 s — a 2x increase in read pressure on the contended shared file, per topic, per bridge process, forever, while the README promises the loop "backs the loop off exponentially (to 30 s)" and the ceiling's own JSDoc says "a down DB is re-probed forever but cheaply". At `poll_interval_ms: 2147483647` the increase is ~71,000x. The shipped table pins this as intended: background-jobs.test.ts rows `{ pollIntervalMs: 60_000, failures: 10, expected: CEILING_MS }` and `{ pollIntervalMs: MAX_POLL_INTERVAL_MS, failures: 11, expected: CEILING_MS }`.
remediation: Make the ceiling a floor-preserving cap: `return Math.max(pollIntervalMs, Math.min(pollIntervalMs * 2 ** doublings, BACKOFF_CEILING_MS));`. Then update the two table rows and the README sentence to say the degraded delay is the configured interval or 30 s, whichever is LONGER — the ceiling bounds recovery latency only for intervals below it, which is the only regime where it can.

The existing `never decreases as failures accumulate, and never exceeds the ceiling` case is too narrow precisely because it asserts only the upper bound; the missing half is the lower one.

summary: shedCrowdedest's per-client tier degenerates to plain oldest-first FIFO when every client holds exactly one pending consent, so an anonymous flood using a distinct client_id per /authorize evicts the owner's in-flight consent — the exact lockout the module comment says the tier exists to prevent.
failure: Owner's Claude does GET /authorize first (pending = [ownerConsent]); an anonymous caller then registers 100 clients and issues one /authorize each. On the 100th insert map.size is 101, every client holds n=1, so `n > (held.get(crowdedest) ?? 0)` is true only for the FIRST client iterated — the owner's, because a Map iterates in insertion order. victim = the owner's consentId. The owner then POSTs the correct passphrase to /parley/consent and gets 403 'consent request expired or unknown'. Reproduced directly against ParleyOAuthProvider: completeConsent(ownerConsent, GOOD_PASS) rejects with ConsentError after the flood.
remediation: Break count ties toward the client whose entries are the MOST RECENT rather than the first-iterated, and call shedCrowdedest(this.pending, MAX_PENDING - 1, ...) BEFORE this.pending.set in ParleyOAuthProvider.authorize so the arriving entry is never the victim. With both changes the oldest pending entry is structurally protected: with a single-client flood the tier still fires (count 99 > 1) and sheds the flooder's oldest; with a distinct-client flood the shed lands on the newest existing entry, which is always a flood entry.
testUpgrade: The class is 'an anonymous flood displaces owner state that is mid-creation'. The existing table at oauth-provider.test.ts:1392 crosses capped store x arrival order but hardcodes ONE flood shape per store, with the load-bearing comment 'One registration is enough: /authorize is per-address rate limited, not per client_id'. Add a third axis — flood SHAPE — with at least {single client_id, one distinct client_id per entry, distinct client_id plus a second entry for one of them} and run every capped store x arrival order x shape, asserting the owner's entry is still redeemable. Also retire the oldest-first wording in 'pending stays bounded when driven past its cap, shedding oldest-first' (oauth-provider.test.ts:383) for the pending row: that assertion is the defect written down as a requirement.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Map insertion-order iteration in shedCrowdedest (`for (const [key, value] of map)`) and the fact that `authorize` is the only writer of `pending`. It relies on the existing `oldestOf` bookkeeping staying oldest-keyed while only the crowdedest SELECTION changes.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: An owner pending consent created before an anonymous distinct-client flood of any size now survives to completeConsent.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: When the map is full and every client holds one entry, the most recently created pending consent is shed instead of the oldest — so a caller who is last in a tie loses its consent, where today it kept it.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: I applied the fix and ran the auth suite: exactly one test fails, oauth-provider.test.ts:383 'pending stays bounded when driven past its cap, shedding oldest-first', at `expect(peek(p)[s.store].has(keys[0]!)).toBe(false)` — the first-inserted pending entry now survives, which is the intended behaviour. The four cells of 'an anonymous flood never displaces state the owner is mid-way through creating' stay green, and my distinct-client probe goes green.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the bug remained, nothing: shedding is the only path that removes a live pending consent before its TTL, so changing the victim selection is the fix rather than a mask. It does NOT fix the sibling finding on the clients map, which uses a different selector.

summary: evictionCandidate's second pass returns the FIRST un-approved client id, so when every registration holds anonymous-tier state the owner's registration — created first — is the one dropped, invalidating the consent page they are currently looking at.
failure: Owner's client registers and does /authorize (holding only pending state, which clientStates() marks ownerApproved:false by design). An anonymous caller then registers 100 clients and issues one /authorize for each. On registration 101, `ids.find((id) => !anyState.has(id))` returns undefined (every client now holds pending state) and `ids.find((id) => !approved.has(id))` returns ids[0] = the owner's client. Reproduced: `p.clientsStore.getClient('owner-claude')` returns undefined after the flood. The owner submits the correct passphrase, gets a 302 with a code, and the client's POST /token then fails invalid_client because authenticateClient can no longer resolve the client_id.
remediation: In evictionCandidate, make the second pass `ids.findLast((id) => !approved.has(id))` so the most recently registered un-approved client is dropped instead of the longest-standing one. The first pass (a registration holding no state at all) is unchanged and still takes priority.
testUpgrade: Same class and same table as the sibling finding: the flood-shape axis added at oauth-provider.test.ts:1392 must apply to the clients row too, and its check must be 'the owner's registration is still resolvable AND the consent it is mid-way through still completes', not merely getClient() !== undefined. The current clients flood (`registerOn(p)(makeClient('spam-'+i))`) creates registrations with NO state, which can never reach the second pass — so that row cannot fail for this defect no matter how large the flood.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `ids` being `[...this.clients.keys()]` in Map insertion order, and registerClient choosing the victim from EXISTING keys before inserting the newcomer (`!this.clients.has(full.client_id) && this.clients.size >= MAX_CLIENTS`), so findLast can never select the client currently being registered.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: An owner registration that predates a stateful anonymous flood survives it.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: The most recently registered un-approved client is evicted where today the oldest was — a second legitimate connector registering during a flood can now be displaced by a third.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I applied `findLast` and ran the whole auth suite: 15 files / 948 tests all pass. I specifically checked oauth-provider.test.ts:383 (its clients flood creates stateless registrations, so it still resolves in the first pass) and the four cells of the anonymous-flood table.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing stays broken that this hides: the second pass is the only code that can delete a registration holding owner-relevant state. It does NOT address the pending-map lockout, which is a separate selector.

summary: assertOidcPolicy claims to restate 'every rule the config schema puts on the auth.oidc block' but omits required_scope, and the schema's own z.string().min(1) accepts whitespace — so a blank required_scope boots a healthy-looking resource server that 403s every valid token forever, the precise failure mode the function's docstring says it exists to prevent.
failure: auth.oidc.required_scope = '   ' passes parseConfig (min(1) counts three spaces) and passes assertOidcPolicy. createOidcRemoteApp then sets `requiredScope: '   '` on the verifier and publishes `scopes_supported: ['   ']` in the Protected Resource Metadata. OidcTokenVerifier computes scopes as `payload.scope.split(' ').filter(Boolean)`, which can never contain a blank token, so a correctly minted token with scope 'mcp openid profile' gets 403 insufficient_scope. Reproduced end to end against the fake IdP: PRM scopes_supported = ["   "], POST /mcp with a valid Bearer returns 403 instead of 200. `required_scope: ''` reaches the same place through the public factory, which the file header names as the reason these checks exist.
remediation: Add a required_scope branch to assertOidcPolicy alongside the audience one (`if (oidc.required_scope !== undefined && !isNonBlank(oidc.required_scope)) throw ...`), and tighten OidcAuthSchema's required_scope to a trimmed non-empty string so parseConfig refuses whitespace too. A scope token is 1*NQCHAR per RFC 6749 §3.3, so a value containing a space can never match a split(' ') token either — refusing any required_scope with internal whitespace is the strict and correct rule.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a factory check that mirrors a schema rule mirrors only some of its keys'. OIDC_VALUE_ROWS in invariants.test.ts:167 is hand-enumerated over five keys. Derive the row set from OidcAuthSchema's shape keys instead — assert `new Set(OIDC_VALUE_ROWS.map(r => r.key))` equals the schema's non-structural keys, so a key with no degenerate-value row is a red row rather than a silent hole — and add the degenerate corpus ['', ' ', '\t', 'a b'] for every string-valued key including required_scope, audience, issuer and jwks_uri.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `isNonBlank` already in invariants.ts (`typeof value === 'string' && value.trim() !== ''`) and the fact that createOidcRemoteApp only forwards requiredScope when `oidc.required_scope !== undefined`, so undefined stays the no-gate case.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: auth.oidc.required_scope values of '', ' ', '\t' — configurations that boot today and then 403 every token.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I applied the assertOidcPolicy half and ran the auth suite: 15 files / 948 tests pass. I checked that oidc-remote.test.ts's required_scope cases use 'mcp' and 'parley' (non-blank) and that OIDC_VALUE_ROWS has no required_scope row at all, so nothing pins the current lenient behaviour. The schema half was not run and could break a fixture that relies on min(1) alone; I did not find one.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the boot check were added but the verifier still compared against a raw untrimmed scope, an operator writing 'mcp ' (trailing space) would still 403 everything — isNonBlank passes it. Trimming or rejecting internal whitespace in the schema is what closes that remainder.

summary: The AS-metadata mirror served in delegated mode is lossy: OpenIdProviderDiscoveryMetadataSchema is a plain z.object, so fetchOidcDiscovery strips revocation_endpoint, introspection_endpoint and every vendor field before the mirror is built — a client discovering the IdP through Parley's origin cannot revoke its token.
failure: Boot createOidcRemoteApp against an IdP whose discovery document carries revocation_endpoint, introspection_endpoint and end_session_endpoint (a stock Keycloak realm does). GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server on Parley returns a document with none of them — reproduced: `as.revocation_endpoint` is undefined where the IdP advertises `<issuer>/revoke`. OpenIdProviderMetadataSchema is a looseObject but OpenIdProviderDiscoveryMetadataSchema re-wraps its .shape in z.object, which strips unknown keys, and OAuthMetadataSchema.parse then has nothing left to copy. docs/keycloak-integration.md:46 calls this 'a read-only mirror of the realm's AS metadata' and :193 says 'Token lifetime, refresh, and revocation are Keycloak's' — a pre-RFC-9728 client that believes the mirror has no revocation endpoint to call. Separately, RFC 8414 §3.3 requires a client to check that `issuer` matches the location it fetched the document from, and this document's issuer is the IdP, not this origin.
remediation: Keep the raw discovery JSON and mirror from it: have fetchOidcDiscovery return both the validated metadata and the unparsed body, and build the mirrored document with OAuthMetadataSchema.parse(rawBody) (OAuthMetadataSchema is a looseObject, so it preserves everything it does not name). If a full-fidelity mirror is not wanted, delete the mirror and let RFC 9728 discovery do its job, and correct the two doc paragraphs; a silently-truncated mirror is worse than none because the client cannot tell truncation from absence.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a document Parley republishes on behalf of another server loses fields nobody asserted'. Give the fake IdP in src/testing/fake-oidc.ts a discovery document carrying the full stock-Keycloak field set, then assert field-by-field equality between what the IdP serves at /.well-known/openid-configuration and what Parley serves at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server — a set-difference assertion over the JSON keys, not a spot check of issuer and token_endpoint (which is all oidc-remote.test.ts:112 does today). Drive the same assertion from the keycloak e2e so the real realm's field set is graded too.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: OAuthMetadataSchema being `z.looseObject` in @modelcontextprotocol/sdk/dist/esm/shared/auth.js:43 (I read it and confirmed it passes unknown keys through), and mcpAuthMetadataRouter serving `options.oauthMetadata` verbatim (router.js:98).
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: Discovery documents whose extra fields survive into the mirror — every vendor extension the IdP publishes is now republished.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none directly; but republishing raw IdP fields verbatim widens what an issuer-controlled document can put on Parley's origin, so the raw body should still be schema-validated (which OAuthMetadataSchema.parse does) rather than passed through unparsed.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — oidc-remote.test.ts:112 asserts only issuer and token_endpoint, and the fake IdP publishes no field that would newly appear. I did not apply this fix, because it changes fetchOidcDiscovery's return type and therefore its public export signature.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the mirror were widened while the RFC 8414 issuer-vs-location mismatch remained, a strict client would still reject the document — it would simply reject a more complete one. Deciding whether to keep the mirror at all is the part that closes both.

summary: The fake IdP's discovery document is explicitly built to carry 'just enough fields to satisfy the SDK's OAuthMetadataSchema', so the offline suite structurally cannot observe what the delegated-mode mirror drops — and the live Keycloak e2e never asserts the mirror body either, so no tier grades it.
failure: fake-oidc.ts serves exactly issuer, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, jwks_uri, response_types_supported, subject_types_supported, id_token_signing_alg_values_supported, code_challenge_methods_supported, grant_types_supported. Every one of those survives OpenIdProviderDiscoveryMetadataSchema. The three fields the schema strips — revocation_endpoint, introspection_endpoint, and vendor extensions — are absent from the fixture, so oidc-remote.test.ts's mirror assertion passes against a document that has nothing to lose. keycloak.e2e.test.ts:196 asserts only that PRM points at the realm issuer. Result: a real functional loss ships with the suite green at both tiers.
remediation: Extend the fake IdP's discovery document to the stock Keycloak field set (revocation_endpoint, introspection_endpoint, end_session_endpoint, device_authorization_endpoint, *_auth_methods_supported), and let callers override it, so the fake can reproduce the server semantics the code under test actually meets.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a fake that cannot express the input shape the defect needs'. Rather than adding fields ad hoc, drive the fake's discovery document from a checked-in capture of a real Keycloak realm document and assert in fake-oidc's own test that its field set is a superset of the SDK's OAuthMetadataSchema keys — so a schema the SDK later widens, or an endpoint Keycloak later adds, arrives as a red row rather than as a fixture nobody updated.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Nothing in the fake's mint() path — the discovery handler and the JWT minter are independent, so widening the document cannot change any token-verification row.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I checked every consumer of startFakeOidc (oidc-remote, oidc-verifier, oidc-token-kinds, oidc-verifier-wiring, teardown, error-surface, invariants tests); all read only issuer and jwksUri off the returned handle, and none assert the discovery document's key set. Widening it is additive.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Widening the fake alone fixes nothing — it only makes the mirror defect visible. Without the mirror fix the suite would go red, which is the point.

summary: OIDC_VALUE_ROWS is the guard for 'a factory check that mirrors a schema rule must mirror ALL of it', but its subject is a hand-written list of five keys rather than being derived from OidcAuthSchema — so a key with no row is invisible, which is exactly how the blank required_scope hole survived.
failure: OidcAuthSchema declares eight keys (issuer, audience, jwks_uri, required_scope, allowed_subjects, allowed_usernames, required_role, clock_skew_s). OIDC_VALUE_ROWS covers five. required_scope and jwks_uri have no degenerate-value row at all, and the test named 'a factory check that mirrors a schema rule must mirror all of it' passes while assertOidcPolicy mirrors neither. Adding a ninth key to the schema tomorrow produces zero new rows and zero failures.
remediation: Derive the row set from the schema: assert that the set of keys appearing in OIDC_VALUE_ROWS equals `Object.keys(OidcAuthSchema.shape)` minus any explicitly-exempt list, and generate the degenerate corpus per key from its zod type (string -> ['', ' ', '\t']; array-of-string -> [[], [''], ['ok','']]; number -> [-1, max+1, NaN, Infinity, 1.5]).
testUpgrade: The class is 'a ratchet whose subject is a hand list rather than the artefact it audits'. The same shape already appears correctly twice in this package — oauth-provider.test.ts:1146 derives CLIENT_STATES from the provider's own Map fields and :1451 derives the cap rows from eviction.ts's MAX_* exports — so make OIDC_VALUE_ROWS derive from OidcAuthSchema.shape the same way, with a completeness assertion that fails on an unmatched key rather than skipping it.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: OidcAuthSchema being exported from config-auth.ts and being a plain ZodObject with an accessible `.shape` (it is: `z.object({...}).strict()`).
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A schema key with no degenerate-value row now fails the completeness assertion — today required_scope and jwks_uri would both fail until rows are written for them.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: The completeness assertion itself would be red on landing, until required_scope rows are added and jwks_uri is either given rows or explicitly exempted (its transport rule is checked by assertTrustRootUrl, which invariants.test.ts:958 already covers). No other test reads OIDC_VALUE_ROWS.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while assertOidcPolicy still ignores required_scope, the suite goes red and stays red — which is the correct outcome, not a mask.

summary: The security-header block that exists, by its own comment, to cover the browser-facing OAuth consent page sends X-Frame-Options, a frame-ancestors-only CSP, Referrer-Policy and HSTS — but not X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and the CSP carries no script-src or default-src, so the credential-bearing surface has no second line of defence behind escapeHtml.
failure: POST /register echoes the client-supplied client_name and redirect_uris back in a 201 application/json body with no nosniff header; the terminal error handler answers text/plain. A user agent that content-sniffs can render either as HTML. There is no nosniff header anywhere in the repository (grep across packages/, examples/, docs/ returns nothing). Independently, if any interpolation in consent-page.ts ever escaped an attacker-supplied value incompletely, the CSP would permit the resulting inline script, because the only directive present is frame-ancestors 'none'.
remediation: Add `res.setHeader('X-Content-Type-Options', 'nosniff')` to the same middleware, and extend the CSP for the HTML responses to `default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'none'`. The consent page's inline <style> needs style-src 'unsafe-inline'; the `javascript:history.back()` link in renderConsentRefusal will stop working under such a CSP and should become a plain link or be dropped.
testUpgrade: The class is 'the security-header set is asserted by a hand-written list inside one happy-path test'. remote.test.ts:198 checks four headers inline. Replace that with a REQUIRED_HEADERS table (name -> matcher) driven across every front door x every browser-reachable route (/authorize, /parley/consent success and refusal, /register, /token, /revoke, /mcp, both 2xx and 4xx), so a header added for one page is proven present on all of them and a header silently dropped is a red row.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The app-wide middleware at http.ts:114 already running before configureApp and therefore before mcpAuthRouter, which is what makes it reach the SDK's own responses.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Under the tightened CSP, the `javascript:` link in renderConsentRefusal stops working, and any future inline <script> on these pages is blocked.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found for the nosniff half — I grepped for header assertions and only remote.test.ts:198 and the oidc equivalents check headers, all with `.toBe`/`.toContain` on the four existing names, none asserting the absence of others. The CSP half would break remote.test.ts:198's `expect(...).toContain("frame-ancestors 'none'")` only if the directive were reordered out; toContain survives an extended policy.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is currently broken by the absence — escapeHtml is correct and I mutated it (dropping the quote escape kills four tests). This is defence in depth, so applying it while some future escaping bug existed would reduce but not eliminate that bug's impact.

summary: createRemoteAuthApp returns a union whose close()/listen() semantics silently depend on cfg.auth.mode — terminal in builtin mode, idempotent and re-listenable in oidc mode — and RemoteAuthServer, the type the selector actually hands back, documents neither.
failure: A composition root written against RemoteAuthServer that does `await server.close(); ... await server.listen(port)` (a config-reload or a restart-on-signal shape) works in oidc mode and throws 'this remote auth app has been closed and cannot listen again' in builtin mode. The divergence is stated only on OAuthRemoteServer (remote.ts:40) and encoded per-row in teardown.test.ts's `afterClose` field; nothing on the selector or its return type tells the caller which one they hold, and TypeScript cannot narrow the union without a mode check the caller would have to invent.
remediation: Either surface the contract on the type — add a discriminant such as `readonly reusable: boolean` (or `mode: 'builtin' | 'oidc'`) to RemoteAuthServer so the caller can branch, with the terminal/re-listenable rule documented on RemoteAuthServer itself — or make both modes terminal, which is the safer default for a factory whose builtin half releases state listen() does not re-acquire.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a union return type whose members disagree about a contract the caller cannot inspect'. teardown.test.ts already has the right table; extend its Factory row to assert the contract is DISCOVERABLE — i.e. that the value the row calls `afterClose` is readable off the returned server (a discriminant field or a documented mode) rather than being knowledge that lives only in the test — so a third factory cannot land with a third silent contract.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: createRemoteAuthApp already knowing cfg.auth.mode at the point it constructs either server, so the discriminant costs one extra property on each Object.assign.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none behaviourally; adding a required property to RemoteAuthServer would be a compile-time break for anyone hand-constructing the type, which nothing in this repo does.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — teardown.test.ts reads only listen/close/provider/resource off the returned value, and error-surface.test.ts types its Booted.server as RemoteAuthServer and calls only listen/close. Making both modes terminal instead would break teardown.test.ts:154's oidc row, which asserts the second listen succeeds and re-arms an interval.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Documenting the divergence without changing it leaves the astonishment in place for anyone who does not read the type; that is why the discriminant, not a doc line, is the remediation.

summary: redirectUriWasSupplied reads req.query as well as req.body, but the SDK's authorize handler reads only ONE of them per method — so a POST /authorize whose URL happens to carry redirect_uri is recorded as 'client-supplied' even though the SDK ignored it and defaulted, making redirect_uri mandatory at /token for a client that never sent one.
failure: POST /authorize?redirect_uri=https://app.example/cb with client_id, response_type, code_challenge etc. in the urlencoded body. authorize.js:79 parses `req.body` for POST, finds no redirect_uri, and defaults it from the client's single registered URI. redirectUriWasSupplied reads `req.query.redirect_uri`, returns true, and the code record is stored with redirectUriSupplied: true. The client — which believes it never sent redirect_uri — omits it at /token, so `(rec.redirectUriSupplied || redirectUri !== undefined) && redirectUri !== rec.redirectUri` is true and exchangeAuthorizationCode throws InvalidGrantError. The owner has already spent the passphrase and the code is already burned, leaving only a generic invalid_grant — the exact outcome the function's own docstring says the leniency exists to avoid.
remediation: Read the same container the SDK read: `req.method === 'POST' ? req.body : req.query`. That keeps the strict answer for every request the SDK actually honoured and removes the one case where 'supplied' is recorded for a parameter the SDK discarded.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a helper reads a request container the framework did not consult for this method'. Parameterize the existing 'redirect_uri is bound at /token exactly when the client bound it at /authorize' suite (oauth-provider.test.ts:674) over method x container: {GET, POST} x {query only, body only, both, neither}, asserting that the /token binding matches what the SDK's handler saw, not what any container held.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: authorize.js:79 and :123 both branching on `req.method === 'POST' ? req.body : req.query` — I read both; the SDK never mixes the two.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A POST /authorize carrying redirect_uri only in the query string now completes at /token without the client re-sending it.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — every case where the SDK actually read a redirect_uri still records 'supplied'.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — oauth-provider.test.ts's fakeRes() builds `{ method: 'GET', query, body: {} }`, so every existing row is a GET and would be unaffected; crypto-wiring.test.ts uses the same shape. The 'treats an unreadable authorization request as having supplied it' row (oauth-provider.test.ts:698) passes res with no req and is untouched by the method branch.

The reconnect lands at ~600ms and re-LISTENs the channel, but the call returns the row only at 4006ms. Through the MCP surface `blockMs` is core's `catchup.block_max_ms` (default 60000) passed as `remaining`, so one failover stalls a `parley_fetch_recent` for up to 60s and returns an empty page.

summary: `connect()` arms `this.connecting` before its first await and clears it only in its own `finally`. `disconnect()` clears `stopped`, `epoch`, the pool, the listener and every registry — but not `connecting`. So while a slow `connect()` is still in flight, a caller who does exactly what the error tells them to do gets refused again, with a message that states something false ('already connected') and gives advice they have just followed ('call disconnect() first').
failure: Mocked-pg repro (written, run, deleted): `const p = plugin.connect(cfg)` (pool.connect() parked); `await plugin.disconnect()`; `await plugin.connect(cfg)` rejects with `parley-postgres: already connected (or a connect() is still in flight) — call disconnect() first. …`. The plugin holds no pool and no listener at that moment. A supervisor restarting a bridge whose database is unreachable (pg has no `connectionTimeoutMillis` here, so `pool.connect()` can sit for the OS TCP timeout) sees this on every retry until the abandoned attempt finally fails.
remediation: Make the in-flight claim lifecycle-scoped rather than a bare boolean: record the epoch (or a token) the in-flight `connect()` owns, have `disconnect()` invalidate it, and have the guard refuse only for a claim belonging to the CURRENT epoch. Clear it in `open()`'s `finally` only when the token is still ours. Separately, pass `connectionTimeoutMillis` to `new Pool` so the abandoned attempt is bounded — `test/pg-harness.ts` already uses that option for `isUp`.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a lifecycle guard that disconnect() does not release'. Add a table to `connection-hygiene.test.ts`'s out-of-order SEQUENCES driven over {which connect-phase is parked: pool.connect, bootstrap query, advisory lock} x {caller: disconnect-then-connect, disconnect-then-post}, asserting that after `disconnect()` a fresh `connect()` SUCCEEDS while the previous attempt is still parked, and that exactly one lifecycle is published afterwards. The existing 'connect;disconnect;connect' sequence awaits each call, so it can never enter the window; the concurrent-connect matrix fires calls in parallel but never interposes a disconnect.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `this.epoch` (state.ts:661) which `disconnect()` already increments, and `open()`'s existing post-bootstrap check `if (this.stopped || epoch !== this.epoch) { await pool.end(); throw … }` — that is what stops the abandoned attempt from publishing into the successor lifecycle, and my fix depends on it holding.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: `connect(); [not awaited] disconnect(); connect()` now admits the second connect and publishes a working lifecycle.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Nothing new. The refusal for a genuine double-connect within one lifecycle is unchanged.

The token/epoch scoping is what avoids that; I traced it but did not implement and run it.

summary: `assertStorable` refuses NUL bytes and unpaired surrogates so no agent-supplied field renders a raw driver string — the contract `hostile-input.test.ts` states. The file fails with a driver error rather than reporting the plugin gap, and a reviewer reads it as a regression in the plugin. In the other direction, the 1 MB row is routed away from `inReplyTo`, which is unindexed and would have stored it — that field is silently untested at size.

summary: `loginIncomplete` is `this.token === undefined && !this.stopped && !this.loggingIn`, and its JSDoc says the throw exists so a plugin with no credential 'fails naming the cause rather than issuing anonymous requests to the newly configured homeserver and serving whatever a permissive one answers as though it were connected'. `disconnect()` produces exactly that state — token cleared, `stopped: true` — and the `!this.stopped` clause deliberately excludes it, so seam calls after a teardown do issue anonymous requests. `post()` even RESOLVES against a permissive server, and `subscribe()` resolves as a silent no-op (its `isStale` gate returns only after the round-trips), leaving the caller believing it has a live route.

Only `fetchRecent` fails, and with a misleading message ('the plugin disconnected or reconnected mid-call'). In production this is the SIGTERM race: cli.ts's `shutdown` calls `bridge.shutdown()` while an in-flight `parley_post` tool call is still executing.
remediation: Make the no-credential refusal cover the torn-down state as well — drop `!this.stopped` from `loginIncomplete` and let the message distinguish 'connect() has not completed' from 'this plugin was disconnected' — or gate each seam entry point on `isStale(this.generation)` before it touches the network, so `post`/`subscribe` fail fast rather than resolving. Whichever is chosen, `subscribe()` resolving without starting a loop is the astonishing half and should become a rejection.

Add a table `entryPoint(post|fetchRecent|subscribe|resolveIdentity) x teardown(disconnect|bare reconnect|failed connect)` asserting (a) the call rejects naming `[parley-matrix]`, and (b) `fake.requestAuth.slice(mark)` is `[]` — i.e. NOTHING went on the wire, authenticated or not. `reconnect-lifecycle.fake.test.ts`'s 'connect() resets the credential it is replacing' table already makes exactly that pair of assertions, but only for the failed-login cell; the `disconnect()` cell is the one missing, and its `POST_TEARDOWN_FORBIDDEN` regex deliberately permits `/join` and `/send` post-teardown, which is what lets this through.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `MatrixSession.http` (session.ts:314-354) — the `if (this.loginIncomplete) throw` at line 327, which runs before the `Authorization` header is set; and `MatrixParking.standDown` (park.ts:39-54), which is what leaves `token === undefined` with `stopped === true`.

So `fetchRecent({topic})` on a room with plenty of history returns fewer than `limit` messages, or none at all, purely because of what the archive TAIL is made of. Prosody's mod_muc_mam archives subject changes (and XEP-0424/0308 retractions/corrections) with no body, so this is an ordinary room shape, not a hostile one.

summary: When a join CREATES the room (status 201), `onPresence` holds the join promise open across `configureRoom`, whose two owner-config IQs each carry `MAM_TIMEOUT_MS` (15 s) — the same budget as `JOIN_TIMEOUT_MS` (15 s), and started strictly LATER than the join timer. The inner call can therefore outlive the outer deadline, so the creating join rejects with "MUC join timeout" even though occupancy was granted milliseconds in.

Reproduced under fake timers. `ensureJoinedRoom` then evicts the cache, so a later call recovers — but for `subscribe` the rejection is what core's startPushLoop rethrows (the reason rooms.ts:300-303 exists), taking the bridge process down during startup on a MUC that is merely slow to unlock a room.
remediation: Do not run a second 15 s operation inside a 15 s deadline. Either restart/extend the join's deadline when status 201 arrives (bounding the extension by configureRoom's own budget), or resolve the join on the self-presence and gate only the first `post` on the configure promise — a locked room bounces a post anyway, and that bounce names the real condition.

That guards the class 'an inner IO budget that is not strictly smaller than the outer one it nests inside', which recurs anywhere a handshake is completed by a second round trip; today `ownerConfig: 'times-out'` rejects instantly, so no row can express latency at all.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `joinOnce`'s `timer` closure and `settle` (rooms.ts:270-287) — `settle` already clears the timer on both paths, so restarting it is safe; and `configureRoom`'s two `iqCaller.request(..., MAM_TIMEOUT_MS)` calls, whose combined worst case is 30 s, not 15.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: nothing, provided the extension is bounded. An unbounded restart would let a MUC that answers 201 and then never answers the config submit hold the join open for configureRoom's full budget ON TOP of the join's.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — diagnostics.test.ts's durability rows use `ownerConfig: 'times-out'`, which the fake rejects synchronously, so a deadline change cannot move them; read-path-creation asserts only counts of presences and submits. I did NOT run the package suite against this change, so treat it as unverified.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes the spurious join timeout. If applied while the defect remained (e.g. only the second fallback IQ were shortened), a MUC slow on the FIRST submit would still fail the creating join, and a `subscribe` would still take the bridge down.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The orderings that matter: (1) 201 arrives, config resolves, join resolves — unchanged; (2) 201 arrives, join deadline fires, config resolves later — today the join is already rejected and `pending.resolve()` is a no-op; with the fix the deadline has been restarted, so only the config outcome settles it; (3) two callers on the new path — `ensureJoinedRoom` caches one promise per room and `joinOnce`'s `settleFrom` hands a superseded entry the successor's outcome, so a second caller entering during the extended window joins the same single promise and cannot restart the timer twice for itself.

summary: requireSendableBody screens the trailing strip with JavaScript's `\s`, but the server it cites (`zerver/lib/message.py::normalize_body`, `body.rstrip()`) uses Python's `str.isspace()`. Enumerated exhaustively over the whole code space, Python isspace = \p{White_Space} + U+001C..U+001F (29 code points); JS \s = \p{White_Space} - U+0085 + U+FEFF (25). The two sets disagree in BOTH directions, so the function fails at the one job its own JSDoc gives it. The topic half of the identical class already picked \p{White_Space} deliberately for exactly this reason (SERVER_STRIPPED_TOPIC_EDGE, line 46), so the divergence is internal to one file.
failure: post(topic, handle, 'hand-off') -> returns a durable BackendMsgId, and Zulip stored 'hand-off'; the next fetchRecent reads back a body that is not the one post acknowledged (same for U+001C, U+001D, U+001E, U+001F). Conversely post(topic, handle, 'hand-off﻿') -> throws "Zulip rewrites a message body on send: it strips trailing whitespace", naming a rewrite the server never performs; that hand-off can never be posted. Both reproduced by direct unit call against src/wire.ts.
remediation: Replace the two `/\s+$/u` occurrences in requireSendableBody (the strip on line 128 AND the `edge` attribution on line 139, which misnames the offending edge if only one is changed) with the exact Python set `/[\p{White_Space}-]+$/u`. Fix test/fake-zulip.ts::normalizeBody in the same change so the model and the plugin agree on the server, not on each other.

summary: assertGeneration's JSDoc states the house rule: "Keep every seam call on this after the awaits it makes, so that one parked in a request across a disconnect()/connect() cannot resume on the NEXT connection." close() is the one method exempted, and it is the longest-running one. After `await Promise.race([allSettled(exits), delay(TEARDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS)])` it reads and clears `this.queues`, calls `this.rest.deleteQueue(...)` on whatever transport is current by then, awaits again, and finally writes `this.connected = false` — none of it guarded. deleteQueueDetached, ten lines below, pins `rest` for precisely this reason ("so that a delete racing a reconnect drops the queue on the server that minted it instead of offering its id to whatever replaced that connection"); close() does not.
failure: Reproduced. With `DELETE /api/v1/events` black-holed (an explicit row in operability.test.ts's SERVER_STATES, so a modelled state, not an invented one): subscribe, then issue `plugin.disconnect()` WITHOUT awaiting it, then `await plugin.connect({site_url})`, then `await plugin.post(topic2, ..., 'works right after connect')` -> succeeds. Then await the earlier disconnect and post again -> `Error: ZulipPlugin not connected — call connect() first`. The stale close's 2s AbortSignal.timeout expires and it writes connected=false onto the connection that replaced it; every later seam call fails permanently until another connect(). The same window has close() sweeping `this.queues` with `this.rest`, i.e. offering the dead connection's queue ids to the live transport. Reachability caveat, stated plainly: core's stdio-bridge awaits both connect and disconnect (transport/stdio-bridge.ts:67 and releaseAll), so this needs an embedder or operator who does not await disconnect() — the plugin offers no reentrancy guard against that.
remediation: Capture `const generation = this.generation` and `const rest = this.rest` at the top of close(), and guard every post-await step: sweep and delete via the captured `rest`, and make the final `this.connected = false` conditional on `this.generation === generation`. That mirrors what deleteQueueDetached already does one method down.
testUpgrade: CONNECTION_ENDINGS in harness.ts enumerates three ways a connection ends and every one of them awaits the disconnect, so no row can reach this. Widen the dimension rather than adding a case: add an `awaited: boolean` axis to CONNECTION_ENDINGS and cross the existing subscription-lifecycle tables with it, asserting after each ending that the plugin is usable (a post round-trips) and that no queue minted by the NEW connection was deleted. Crossed with the existing TARGETS (same server / a different server) that also catches a stale close deleting a queue id on the wrong server, which is the second half of the same window.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: open()'s `this.generation++` (connection.ts:78) — the guard is only meaningful because open() bumps before it sets connected=true. It also relies on close() itself bumping (line 92), so two concurrent close() calls make the first bail at its own guard, which is the correct outcome.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A connect() landing while a previous close() is still in its queue sweep now survives with connected=true and its queues intact.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: I did not run the fix, so this is where I am least sure. It should not fire, because that test never supersedes the connection mid-close — but a naive guard placed BEFORE the sweep rather than only before `connected = false` would break it, and that is the likely wrong way to apply this.

summary: plaintextRemoteServer() decides whether a credential is on the wire in the clear from the `servers` URL scheme, but nats.js's node transport strips the scheme in `hostPort()` and decides TLS solely from `options.tls` plus the server's INFO. `tls://`, `wss://` and every unrecognised scheme therefore return `undefined` (= no risk) and suppress the warning without buying any encryption — and the same function's JSDoc claims the opposite ('Keep an unparseable server on the warned side').
failure: backend_config `{ servers: 'tls://nats.example.com:4222', token: '<secret>' }` against a NATS server that has no TLS configured -> nats.js opens a plain TCP socket and puts the token in the CONNECT frame of the first round trip, and connect() emits ZERO warnings. Reproduced against a throwaway `nats:2.10-alpine -js`: `connect({servers:'tls://127.0.0.1:14222'})` resolved with `protocol.transport.socket.encrypted === undefined`, and `new NatsPlugin().connect({servers:'tls://127.0.0.1:14222', token:'sekrit'})` produced `warnings: []`. Same for `http://`/`gopher://` prefixes: `plaintextRemoteServer('gopher://203.0.113.9:4222') === undefined`.
remediation: Stop keying the classifier on the scheme. `backend_config.tls` is the only signal that actually forces encryption (verified: `connect({servers:'127.0.0.1:14222', tls:{}})` against a non-TLS server throws `NatsError: tls`, so it is fail-fast, not silent). Make plaintextCredentialRisks warn for every non-loopback `servers` entry whenever a credential field is set and `cfg.tls` is unset, dropping PLAINTEXT_SCHEMES entirely; keep only redactUserinfo for the message. If the NGS false positive (`tls://` + `.creds` against a server whose INFO carries `tls_required: true`, where the link genuinely is encrypted) is unacceptable, move the check AFTER `connect()` and decide from `nc.info` rather than from the string.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the existing `cells` table over a SCHEME AXIS THAT INCLUDES UNKNOWN SCHEMES (`tls://`, `wss://`, `http://`, `redis://`, `nats+tls://`, `''`) and assert `warns === (secret && !tls && !loopback)` with no scheme term at all — i.e. the expectation must be independent of the scheme, which is the invariant. Add a live agreement row (in the style of jetstream-agreement.ts) that connects through each scheme to a plaintext throwaway server and asserts the socket the driver actually opened is unencrypted, so the classifier is graded against the driver rather than against a literal list. The existing `it('the plaintext scheme set is exactly nats://, ws:// and a bare host:port')` is the test that is too narrow: it asserts the wrong rule and must be deleted, not widened.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: config.ts `plaintextCredentialRisks`: `if (fields.length === 0 || cfg.tls !== undefined) return [];` — I depend on that `cfg.tls !== undefined` branch staying the suppressor, and on nats.js node_transport.js:74 `checkOptions` throwing `NatsError('tls')` when `options.tls` is set and the server does not offer TLS (reproduced).
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — it only widens a stderr warning; connect() still succeeds. It newly WARNS on `servers: 'tls://remote:4222'` + `token` with `tls` unset, which today is silent.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: config.test.ts 'the plaintext scheme set is exactly nats://, ws:// and a bare host:port'; the ~100 ENCRYPTED_SCHEMES rows of `it.each(cells)('servers $server (secret $secret, tls $tls) warns as documented')`; the `tls://` rows of `it(...)` in 'a credential in the servers URL is refused, never echoed'; and 'warns once per offending entry when servers is a list' (expects 2 warnings, would see 3 once the `tls://b.example.com` entry warns).
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the driver still ignores the scheme, the operator now gets a warning naming the field it would expose — which is the whole mitigation. What stays broken either way: the plugin still cannot PROVE the link is encrypted, so a warning is advice, not enforcement; an operator who wants a guarantee must set backend_config.tls.

summary: validateRetentionDays rejects `0` because 'JetStream reads max_age: 0 as UNLIMITED — the exact opposite of what an operator wrote', but it validates the operator's DAYS and never the `max_age` those days compose in streams.ts (`Math.round(days * NS_PER_DAY)`). Two ranges of finite positive days land back on max_age 0, silently.
failure: Measured against a real nats:2.10-alpine -js: retention_days 1e300 -> stream created with max_age = 0 (UNLIMITED); retention_days 1e-16 -> max_age = 0 (UNLIMITED); retention_days 1e9 -> `NatsError: invalid json` (loud but opaque, naming no field); retention_days 1e-10 -> server rejects with 'max age needs to be >= 100ms'; retention_days 0.5 -> 43200000000000 (correct). The 1e300 case goes Infinity -> JSON.stringify -> `null` -> Go zero value -> 0, so the plugin configures permanent retention on a topic the operator asked to prune, with no error on any surface.
remediation: Validate the composed value rather than the unit: after `const maxAge = Math.round(days * NS_PER_DAY)`, require `Number.isSafeInteger(maxAge) && maxAge >= 100_000_000` (JetStream's own 100ms floor) and reject otherwise, naming retention_days and the max_age it composed — mirroring what validatePrefix already does with its PROBE_TOKEN composition check. Do it in validateRetentionDays (which runs at connect()) so the failure is not deferred to the first post.
testUpgrade: Extend the `retentions` table in config.test.ts with a COMPOSED-VALUE axis rather than more literals: rows for the four boundary classes — rounds to 0 (5e-15), below JetStream's 100ms floor (1e-9), overflows int64 ns (1e9), overflows to Infinity (1e300) — plus a property case asserting for a generated set of accepted `days` that `fake.state.added.max_age` is a safe positive integer <= 2^63-1. The existing rows (0, -0, -1, NaN, ±Infinity, wrong types) are the ones too narrow: every one of them fails before multiplication, so none can reach this class.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: streams.ts:69 `config.max_age = Math.round(this.retentionDays * NS_PER_DAY)` — the only composition site — and NS_PER_DAY = 86_400_000_000_000.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: retention_days values that today connect and then create an unlimited or unparseable stream: anything <= ~1.16e-12 days (under JetStream's 100ms floor), anything >= ~1.07e8 days (int64 ns overflow), and anything >= ~2.08e294 (Infinity). All are configs the server either silently reinterprets or refuses.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — the accepted rows in config.test.ts's `retentions` table are undefined, 30, 1 and 0.5, all of which compose safe integers well above 100ms. I checked each against the proposed bounds.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the underlying rounding stayed, nothing is hidden: the check is on the value actually sent, so it fails fast at connect() naming the field. What remains broken independently: an operator who already created a stream under a bad max_age is unaffected — retention is locked at creation, as the README says.

summary: `streamForRead`'s blocking loop re-runs the FULL `existingStream` — which is `streams.info` AND, on 404, `refuseRivalStream`'s `streams.find` — every ABSENT_STREAM_POLL_MS (250ms) for the whole budget. `streams.find` answers 'does another stream already capture this subject', a question that is an operator-config divergence, not a per-tick condition.
failure: Instrumented against a real server: `fetchRecent({topic: 'never-posted', blockMs: 3000})` issued 13 `streams.info` and 13 `streams.find` calls. At core's default `catchup.block_max_ms` of 60s that is ~240 + ~240 = ~480 JetStream API round trips ($JS.API.STREAM.INFO and $JS.API.STREAM.NAMES) per outstanding long-poll per topic — and a bridge long-polls every allowlisted topic it has not seen a post on, continuously.
remediation: Hoist the divergence check out of the loop: run `refuseRivalStream` on the FIRST miss only and poll with a bare `streams.info` thereafter, and back the poll off (250ms -> 1s -> 2s, capped) rather than holding a fixed 4Hz. Both keep the 'a read never provisions' property that the loop exists for.
testUpgrade: A parameterized cost case over the fake, which already counts calls: for blockMs in {1000, 5000, 30000} x {absent stream, stream appears midway}, assert `streams.find` was called at most once and that `streams.info` calls grow SUB-LINEARLY in blockMs (e.g. <= 2 + log2(blockMs/250)). Written as a budget on call counts rather than on a specific interval, so a future change to the poll schedule is graded by cost rather than by the literal 250. long-poll.test.ts's existing cases assert only that the call returns within its budget — they cannot see what the wait cost the cluster.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: streams.ts `existingStream` (the `isStreamMissing(err)` -> `refuseRivalStream` -> `return undefined` path) and read.ts's loop `if (!blocking || remaining <= 0 || this.stopped) return undefined`.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A rival stream created DURING a long-poll would no longer be reported by that poll — it would be reported by the next read instead.
