remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found by name. resource.test.ts 'a read names stream_prefix when another stream already captures the topic's subject' uses a non-blocking read (blockMs unset), so the first-miss check still fires. long-poll.test.ts asserts wall-clock budgets, not call counts. I did not run the suite against this change.

summary: `delay(ms)` is used as the losing arm of four `Promise.race`es (EphemeralConsumer.reap, the pull closer, and both races in NatsSession.disconnect) and its setTimeout is never cleared when the other arm wins. Every read leaves a live 2s handle behind, and an awaited disconnect() leaves one too, so the event loop stays alive after teardown has returned.
failure: Measured with `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` against a real server: `connect -> fetchRecent -> await disconnect()` goes from 1 to 2 live `Timeout` handles, i.e. a host that awaits disconnect() and expects to exit lingers up to DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS (2000ms). cli.ts hides this by calling `process.exit(0)`, so only library and test embedders see it.
remediation: Give `delay` a cancel handle — `const t = setTimeout(...); race.finally(() => clearTimeout(t))` at each site, or a small `withTimeout(promise, ms)` helper that clears its own timer — and use it at all four sites. `timer.unref()` would also let the process exit but leaves the handle live inside a still-running host, so the clear is the better fix.
testUpgrade: A parameterized teardown-hygiene case: for each seam operation {fetchRecent, blocking fetchRecent, subscribe, post, no-op} run connect -> op -> disconnect and assert `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` holds no more Timeouts than before the connect. Table-driven so a future bounded race added anywhere in the plugin is covered by construction. lifecycle.test.ts's 'an unraced connect() publishes its handles, and disconnect() closes them' is the existing case too narrow: it grades the handles the plugin nulls out, not the ones it leaves running.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: jetstream.ts:11 `export const delay = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms))` and its four race sites: reap()'s `Promise.race([this.adding, delay(DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS)])`, pull.ts's closer `Promise.race([cleanup, delay(DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS)])`, and session.ts's two disconnect races.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — behaviour on the timing path is identical; only the loser's handle is released.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. `delay` is also used as a plain sleep in read.ts's `streamForRead` and live.ts's backoff, where nothing races it — a cancel-capable variant must not replace those, or the sleep becomes a no-op. That is the one way this fix can go wrong.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the timers remained somewhere, the symptom is partial: one uncancelled site is enough to keep the loop alive, so the fix only pays off if all four are converted.
remediationCheck.interleavings: reap()'s race is the one with a real ordering: `Promise.race([adding, delay])` then a check-and-set of `this.reaped`. Clearing the timer in a `.finally` runs after the race settles and before the check-and-set is reached by either racer, so two concurrent reap()s still see the same reaped flag they do today. The pull closer's `Promise.race([cleanup, delay])` is awaited by disconnect() while pull()'s own finally calls cleanedUp() — clearing the loser does not change which arm resolves.

summary: The README tells the operator 'Use `tls://`/`wss://`, or set `tls:`', and config.ts:215 repeats it inside the warning text ('Use tls:// (or wss://), or set backend_config.tls'). The first remedy is inert in the node `nats` package: node_transport.js decides TLS from `options.tls` and the server's INFO, and servers.js `hostPort()` discards the scheme before the connection is made.
failure: An operator who reads the README, changes `servers: 'nats://host'` to `servers: 'tls://host'` and re-runs gets exactly what they were warned about — the credential still in the clear on the CONNECT frame — plus the warning disappearing, which reads as confirmation the problem is solved. Reproduced: `connect({servers:'tls://127.0.0.1:14222'})` gives an unencrypted socket, and the plugin emits no warning for `tls://` + token.
remediation: Rewrite both surfaces to name the only remedy that works: 'set backend_config.tls' (with the note that nats.js then refuses to connect at all if the server cannot do TLS — verified). Say explicitly that the `servers` URL scheme is discarded by nats.js and buys nothing, so a reader cannot re-derive the wrong fix. Land it with the classifier fix so the warning text and the warning's trigger agree.
testUpgrade: docs.test.ts already has the machinery: register 'the scheme in `servers` does not select TLS' as a `serverClaims` row verified by a new AGREEMENT_ROWS entry that connects through each scheme to a plaintext throwaway server and reports whether the socket is encrypted. Then add `tls://` and `wss://` to a banned-remedy list checked across README, the npm description and the warning STRINGS in src/*.ts — the same class as the existing `bannedProperties` screen, extended from 'properties the code defends against' to 'remedies the driver does not honour'.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: config.ts:213-216, the warning template string, and README.md lines 121-125 plus the mapping-table prose. Nothing executable depends on either.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — prose only.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: docs.test.ts 'every README.md claim naming a JetStream primitive is registered' does not police this text (it screens `last_by_subj`/`opt_start_seq`/`first_seq` only), so no existing case reddens. That is itself the reason this claim shipped: the registry covers JetStream primitives and not transport claims.

summary: The package is one class split across six files by a linear inheritance chain — NatsSession -> NatsStreams -> NatsPulls -> NatsReads -> NatsLive -> NatsPlugin — of which five are abstract, none has a second implementation, and none is polymorphic: every `protected` member is called by exactly one layer above it. Inheritance is being used as a file boundary, not as a variation point, and the shared mutable state (`ensured`, `incarnations`, `subscriptions`, `epoch`, `stopped`) stays visible to all six layers because of it.
failure: Not a wrong output — a coupling cost that is already being paid in the tests. Because the seam between the layers is `protected` rather than a parameter, every test that needs to reach it does so through a cast: `injectFake` writes `plugin as unknown as {js, jsm, ensured, incarnations, subject, streamName}`, docs.test.ts casts twice to reach `subject`/`streamName`/`msgId`/`cursorAt`/`incarnations`, and window.test.ts reaches the same members. That is exactly the 'private member reached through a cast' failure mode CLAUDE.md's architectural-test rule names, and it means a rename of any protected member silently turns those probes into assertions about `undefined`.
remediation: Make the layers collaborators rather than ancestors: a `NatsSession` object owning the link and the caches, passed to a `StreamRegistry`, a `Puller` and a `LiveLoop`, with `NatsPlugin` composing them. The immediate, much cheaper half is to give the test seam a name — a small explicit accessor surface (subject/streamName/msgId/cursorAt and a fake-injection point) so no test needs `as unknown as`.
testUpgrade: Guard the class rather than the shape: a lint over `packages/bridge-nats/test/**` asserting no `as unknown as {` cast reaching a plugin member, driven by a list of member names read off `src/**` rather than hard-coded, so a member renamed or moved reddens instead of turning a probe into `expect(undefined).toBeUndefined()`. Note deliberately that this must NOT be written as an assertion about which file a class lives in — CLAUDE.md forbids a ratchet that cements the layout.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The chain as declared: session.ts:17, streams.ts:13 `extends NatsSession`, pull.ts:17 `extends NatsStreams`, read.ts:10 `extends NatsPulls`, live.ts:8 `extends NatsReads`, index.ts:19 `extends NatsLive`. And the casts at fake-jetstream.ts:412, docs.test.ts:27 and :219.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: The full restructure would break `injectFake` (writes `peek.js`/`peek.jsm` directly onto the instance) and therefore every fake-backed file — window, cursor, cursor-input, resource, long-poll, msg-id, subscribe-loop, recovery, lifecycle, config. That is a large blast radius against the protocol's 'a split lands only if the existing tests pass unmodified' rule, which is why I am filing the accessor-surface half as the actionable part and the full recomposition as a judgement call for the orchestrator, not a change to make under a review round.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: The accessor half fixes only the test-coupling symptom; the shared protected state, which is the underlying reason the layers are not independently testable, stays.

summary: One of three full-package runs (against a private nats:2.10-alpine -js on a dedicated port) failed at outage.test.ts:241 — `waitFor(() => got.includes('during-gap'), 60000)` — i.e. the subscribe loop did not redeliver the outage-gap message within 60s. The same file passed 17/17 in isolation, and two later full runs were green, so the trigger is contention with the other 22 files sharing the server, not the row itself.
failure: `backfills the outage gap when <prior> and the <cause>` -> the message published while the subscriber had no consumer never reaches the handler inside 60s. Which of the six rows failed was not captured. A 60s timeout on a loop whose backoff is 1000ms is a stall, not slowness: either a rebuild iteration blocked far longer than its bounded pieces should allow, or the loop stopped rebuilding. I could not reproduce it in two further attempts, so I cannot name the mechanism, and I explicitly do NOT claim `await statusTask` in live.ts:104 as the cause — jetstream-agreement.ts's `watchExit` rows already grade that lifecycle against both the fake and a real server, for both the 'drain' and 'break' exits.
remediation: Make the failure diagnosable before deciding it is a test problem: on timeout, dump the loop's observable state (consumer count on the stream, `nc.isClosed()`, the last `lastSeq` and iteration count) rather than only 'timed out waiting for condition'. If it recurs, bound the two unbounded awaits at the end of each live.ts iteration (`await statusTask` and `await ephemeral.reap()`) with the same DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS race the rest of the teardown path uses, so a stuck watcher costs one iteration instead of the subscription.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a subscribe loop that stops rebuilding is silent': add a liveness assertion available to every outage row — after the heal, assert the loop performed at least one rebuild within N x RESUBSCRIBE_BACKOFF_MS by observing the consumer name changing on the stream — so a stall reports WHERE it stalled instead of only that a message never arrived. Run outage.test.ts in the same worker-contention conditions the full suite creates (or pin it to its own pool) so the flake is reproducible rather than sampled.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: live.ts:104-105 `await statusTask; await ephemeral.reap();` — neither is raced against a timeout, unlike every other await in the teardown path. That is an observation about the code, not evidence that it fired.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A bounded `statusTask` would let the loop rebuild while a status watcher is still pending, so two watchers could briefly overlap on one subscription.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: unknown — I did not apply the bound or run against it. subscribe-loop.test.ts's rebuild rows and resource-live.test.ts 'rebuilding after consumer loss does not stack consumers' are the two most likely to react, the latter because an overlapping watcher is exactly what it counts.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Bounding the awaits would convert a hypothetical permanent stall into a one-iteration delay — but if the real cause is elsewhere (server-side consumer GC, proxy heal timing), it hides nothing and fixes nothing, which is why the diagnostic half comes first.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The orderings that matter: disconnect() landing between `await statusTask` and `await ephemeral.reap()` (today the epoch check after them ends the loop; with a bound, the reap could race the disconnect's own closer, which is already idempotent via EphemeralConsumer.reaped); and a rebuild starting while the previous iteration's watcher still holds the old iterator.

summary: newestWindow interpolates a provider-supplied message id straight into the query string (`&before=${before}`) while its sibling windowSince encodes the same class of value (`after=${encodeURIComponent(...)}`). `hasUsableId` accepts any non-empty string, so a record id carrying `&`, `#` or `?` reshapes the next page request.
failure: fetchRecent({topic:'880001', limit:150}) against a 100-record page whose oldest record has id '300000000000000001&limit=1' issues, as reproduced with the package's own fake: GET /api/v10/channels/880001/messages?limit=50&before=300000000000000001&limit=1 -- a second `limit` parameter the plugin never chose. A `#` in the same position truncates everything after it as a URL fragment.
remediation: Wrap the anchor the same way windowSince already does: `` `limit=${size}&before=${encodeURIComponent(before)}` ``. Better still, build both queries with URLSearchParams so no future anchor can be added unencoded.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a table over HOSTILE_ANCHOR_IDS x {newestWindow (no since), windowSince (since)} that injects a 200 page whose oldest record carries an id from a generator of query-metacharacter payloads ('a&limit=1', 'a#f', 'a?x=1', 'a b', 'a%2F'), then asserts on fake.requests(): every `.../messages` path must parse to exactly one `limit` and one `before`/`after` key, and the decoded anchor must equal the id verbatim. Today's nearest tables cannot see this: rest-contract's HOSTILE_IDS table varies the CHANNEL id (its CHANNEL_ROUTE regex allows any query string), and the malformed-200 table only uses ids that are unusable, so none reaches the interpolation. Grepping the whole suite for 'before=' returns zero assertions.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Nothing new. `walk()` already passes `walked.at(-1)?.id` as the anchor and the fake's handler reads it via `url.searchParams.get('before')`, which decodes percent-escapes -- so an encoded value round-trips to the same id.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: An id containing `&` or `#` now reaches Discord as one opaque `before` value rather than as extra parameters, so Discord answers 400 (not a snowflake) where today it silently serves a differently-shaped page. That is the correct direction but it is a visible behaviour change for a broken upstream.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found -- I applied the one-line change and ran the full package suite: 830 passed. I also grepped test/*.ts for 'before=' and found no assertion on that query at all.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes the interpolation only. `hasUsableId` still accepts any non-empty string as a snowflake, so such an id still crosses the seam as both backendMsgId and cursor and is later fed back as `since` -- that path is encoded, so it is contained, but the cursor itself is still garbage.

summary: A blocking fetchRecent armed under session A is woken by connect()'s forgetTopics() -> wake(waiters), and its continuation then re-queries REST under session B's api_url and token. The `this.stopped = true` guard on line 49 cannot prevent it: connect() has no await, so `stopped` is back to false before any woken continuation runs, and index.ts's post-wake `if (this.stopped ...)` check therefore reads false.
failure: connect({api_url: A}); subscribe(topic); fetchRecent({topic, since:'1', blockMs:5000}); then connect({api_url: B, token:'other-token'}). Reproduced: server B receives exactly one GET /channels/<id>/messages that server A's caller asked for, and the result -- messages and nextCursor minted by a different Discord deployment -- is returned to the session-A caller. Expected: the parked call hands back its empty, replayable page (nextCursor === since) as it does under disconnect().
remediation: Give DiscordSession a `sessionEpoch` counter bumped in both connect() and disconnect(), capture it in fetchRecent before arming the waiter, and widen the post-wake bail to `if (this.stopped || session !== this.sessionEpoch || Date.now() >= deadline) return first;`. The `stopped = true`/`stopped = false` dance in connect() then has no remaining job and should go with it.
testUpgrade: Add a SESSION_TRANSITIONS axis (disconnect(), connect() alone, disconnect()+connect()) crossed with an IN-FLIGHT CALL axis (blocking fetchRecent, catch-up fetchRecent, post, subscribe) driven against TWO distinct fake servers with different tokens, asserting the invariant `the second server sees zero requests attributable to a call started against the first`. gateway-budget.test.ts's 'a long-poll was in flight' cells are too narrow: they assert only that the SECOND session is unaffected and never look at what the FIRST call returned or which server answered it.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The existing post-wake branch `if (this.stopped || Date.now() >= deadline) return first;` in index.ts fetchRecent, and `first` being the empty replayable page `{messages: [], nextCursor: since}` produced by fetchWithin. Both verified in source.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A long-poll that spans a connect() now returns its empty page instead of a page from the new session. Core's fetchRecentBlocking treats that as a normal empty window and polls again with the same `since`, so no message is lost -- it is re-fetched under the new session on the next iteration.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none -- I applied the change (sessionEpoch on DiscordSession, captured in fetchRecent, checked post-wake) and ran the full package suite: 830 passed. I then re-ran the two-server probe and it went from failing to passing.

Result: `Tests 87 passed (87)`. Expected: five failures.

The existing negative control 'ignores banned prose that is code rather than a comment' is what the literal-stripping step must keep passing.

That table would also catch the mid-line block-comment hole, which I did not test but which the same `text.startsWith('/*')` check has.

summary: `handshake_timeout_ms` is taken verbatim into setTimeout while its sibling `gateway_dialers` gets a careful integer>=1 refusal with a message explaining the quota it divides. A 0, a negative, or a YAML string coerces to an immediate watchdog, so every socket is terminated before HELLO and live push is permanently dead after one stderr line at subscribe -- no further diagnostic ever fires.
failure: connect({token, api_url, gateway_url, handshake_timeout_ms: 0}) then subscribe(topic): reproduced one stderr line `parley-discord: live push for topic "880002" is not up yet (Discord gateway handshake timed out after 0ms (no READY)); the reconnect ladder is retrying`, and thereafter fetchRecent({since, blockMs:300}) returns {messages:[],nextCursor:'1'} immediately forever -- the plugin degrades to catch-up-only with no error the operator can act on. Expected, by the package's own precedent: connect() rejects naming the knob.
remediation: Add a `requireHandshakeTimeout(value)` alongside requireReconnectCap in config.ts, refusing anything that is not a finite number >= some floor (the fixtures use 150ms, so a floor of ~50ms is safe), and call it from connect() before anything is installed -- the same position requireDistinctChannels/requireReconnectCap occupy, so a bad value cannot half-retire the previous session.
testUpgrade: Widen the existing `gateway_dialers ${value} is refused at connect` table into a parameterized CONFIG_KNOBS table: (knob, value, refused?) over {gateway_dialers, handshake_timeout_ms} x {0, -1, 1.5, NaN, Infinity, '10', null, undefined} -- one row per knob-value pair, asserting connect() either rejects naming the knob or the default is applied. The current table pins only one knob, so no value of the other one can fail it.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The ordering in DiscordSession.connect: requireDistinctChannels and requireReconnectCap both run BEFORE `this.stopped = true`, so a throw leaves the previous session intact. A new check must go in that same prefix.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: handshake_timeout_ms: 0, negatives, non-integers below the floor, and non-numbers. Note this is a compatibility break for anyone who set 0 deliberately to disable push -- there is no evidence anyone does, and the README documents no such use, but it is a behaviour change from 'silently no push' to 'connect() rejects'.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found -- I grepped every handshake_timeout_ms in test/: the values used are 150, 500, HANDSHAKE_MS, NO_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT (10_000_000) and DEFAULT_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS, all well above any sane floor. I did not implement the check and run the suite, so this is a grep-level rather than executed answer.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes only this knob. The broader gap remains: backend_config arrives from YAML with no schema at all, so channel_map values, allowed_mentions shape and api_url are equally unvalidated at connect and only fail later (or, for allowed_mentions, never).

summary: DiscordSession carries three private getters -- reconnectAttempts, heartbeats, gatewayReady -- that no production code reads. They exist so gateway-budget.test.ts and gateway-reconnect.test.ts can reach ladder state through `(plugin as unknown as {...})` casts, and the comment defending them is written to a future reader who might delete them. CLAUDE.md's standing rule prefers 'a behaviour reachable through the public surface rather than a private member reached through a cast'.
failure: Delete the three getters (lines 110-124) and the suite goes red at gateway-reconnect.test.ts:82 (`(plugin as unknown as {gatewayReady?: unknown}).gatewayReady`), :254 and gateway-budget.test.ts:182 -- not because behaviour changed, but because the cast now reads undefined. That is the same tautology failure mode CLAUDE.md records: an assertion that would silently become `expect(undefined).toBeUndefined()` if the getter were merely renamed rather than removed.
remediation: Have those suites reach the ladder through the object that owns it. The gateway instance is already a `protected readonly` member, so `(plugin as unknown as {gateway: {reconnectAttempts:number; heartbeats:ReadonlySet<NodeJS.Timeout>; ready?:Promise<void>}}).gateway` grades the same state one hop closer to its owner, and the three forwarding getters plus their comment come out of production source.

Every table that reads ladder state then routes through it, so a moved or renamed member fails loudly instead of degrading to undefined.

summary: Every one of the 7 cells ends with an unconditional `await delay(WATCH_MS)` of 1300ms to watch for a request that should never come. That is ~9.1s of the file's measured 9.6s, for a table whose 6 rateLimited rows differ only in which entry point they call. It is the second most expensive file in the package after the 346-cell rest-contract suite.
failure: `npx vitest run packages/bridge-discord --reporter=basic` reports `disconnect-quiescence.test.ts (7 tests) 9617ms` -- 1.37s per test, of which 1.3s is a sleep whose only job is to outlast RETRY_AFTER_S = 1. The sleep discriminates nothing that a shorter, proportionally-derived window would not.
remediation: Derive the watch window from the stated wait instead of hard-coding both, and shrink them together: RETRY_AFTER_S 1 -> 0.3 and WATCH_MS = RETRY_AFTER_S*1000*1.5 (450ms), keeping SETTLE_MS well under it. Same invariant, roughly a third of the wall clock. The margin is genuinely reduced, so the derivation should be written as arithmetic on RETRY_AFTER_S rather than as a second literal, so a later widening of the wait carries the window with it.
testUpgrade: Make the cost structural rather than per-row: keep ONE cell that proves the watch window is long enough to observe a retry (inject the 429, do NOT disconnect, assert the request count DOES grow within WATCH_MS -- a positive control the file currently lacks entirely), and let the other six rows assert only that the count is frozen, using a window derived from RETRY_AFTER_S. Without that positive control, shrinking the window is unfalsifiable: a WATCH_MS too short to have ever seen a retry would make all seven rows pass for the wrong reason.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: net-util's `sleepUnlessStopped`, quoted: it re-reads `isStopped()` every STOP_POLL_MS = 25ms, so a disconnect is observed within 25ms regardless of the stated wait -- SETTLE_MS = 600 has enormous headroom and the shrink does not threaten it.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A retry that lands between the new 450ms window and the old 1300ms one would go unobserved. With retry_after shrunk to 0.3s in the same edit the retry would be due at ~300ms, comfortably inside 450ms -- but that is exactly why the positive control in the testUpgrade is not optional.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found -- RETRY_AFTER_S, SETTLE_MS and WATCH_MS are file-local consts read only by this file (grepped). I did not apply the change and re-run, so the claim that all 7 cells still pass at 0.3s/450ms is untested.

summary: `requireUsableMap('mention_map','a handle', …)` checks only `typeof value === 'string' && length > 0`, but every mention_map value is spliced into content as `@${mapped}` and re-parsed by core's `parseMentions`, and is also used verbatim as `Message.senderHandle`. A value core's handle grammar cannot round-trip is accepted at load and then produces no mention at all, so `live_push.mention_filter` armed on that handle drops every message addressed to it, in silence — the exact failure the mention rewrite exists to prevent (markup.ts:24-33 states it as the reason the rewrite exists).
failure: backend_config `mention_map: {U0BOSS: "@ctx-payments"}` (a natural way to write a handle) -> connect() succeeds; an inbound `hey <@U0BOSS>` yields content `hey @@ctx-payments` and `mentions: []`, and a message from U0BOSS yields `senderHandle: "@ctx-payments"`. Reproduced in-process: `{U0BOSS:'the boss'}` -> mentions ['the']; `{U0DEV:'@dev'}` -> mentions []; `{U0OPS:'_ops'}` -> mentions []. A bridge with mention_filter on delivers nothing and reports no error.
remediation: In `requireUsableMap`, when `configKey === 'mention_map'`, additionally require that the value round-trips core's mention grammar, and name the key in the rejection. Core does not export `isMentionableHandle` from its public index (only `parseMentions`), so either export it (a core change — surface it as a seam gap rather than absorb it) or express the same predicate through the exported parser: `parseMentions('@' + value)[0] === value`. Keep it a load error, consistent with the empty-string/non-string rows already there.
testUpgrade: CLASS: every backend_config map value whose destination has a GRAMMAR, not just a type. Parameterize the existing hostile-input `CONFIG_MAPS x UNUSABLE_TARGETS` table over a generator of handle-shaped strings drawn from core's `src/testing/handle-corpus.ts` (leading `@`, embedded space, leading/trailing `-`/`_`/`.`, non-ASCII, `x!y`), asserting for each that `connect` either rejects naming `mention_map` and the key, or that a message mentioning that id yields `mentions` containing exactly the configured value AND `senderHandle` equal to it. The existing mention-markup ROWS table is too narrow to catch this: every one of its map values is already a valid handle, so no row can discriminate.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `parseMentions` from @sharptrick/parley-core (exported at src/index.ts:23); its regex `(?:^|[^A-Za-z0-9_.@-])@(HANDLE_BODY)`, which anchors at start-of-string for `'@' + value`, so the branch relied on is the `^` alternative. `isMentionableHandle` exists at src/mentions.ts:18 but is NOT in core's public export list, so importing it directly would not compile against the published package.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — the predicate is strictly narrower than the current `non-empty string` check.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `mention_map: {U0BOSS: "@ctx-payments"}`, `{U0X: "the boss"}`, `{U0Y: "_ops"}`, `{U0Z: "bob."}` — all accepted today.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I grepped every mention_map/mentionMap literal in packages/bridge-slack/test: mention-markup.test.ts MENTION_MAP = {U0PARLEY:'ctx-payments', S0OPS:'ops-crew', toString:'meta-mapped'}, vendor-markup.test.ts {U0BOSS:'the-boss', S0OPS:'ops-crew'}, hostile-input.test.ts {U0PARLEY:'alpha'}; every value is mentionable, so all pass the new predicate. The hostile-input UNUSABLE_TARGETS rows ('' , null, 42, true, {}, []) still reject on the existing type check, which must run first so the error text keeps saying "not a handle".

The label fallback at markup.ts:46 is the remaining hole and would need its own decision.

summary: `blockForMessage` arms a waiter, then `await this.runFetch(...)`. Every exit that returns calls `wake()` or is drained by `stop()`, but the exit where `runFetch` REJECTS does not: the rejection propagates out of `blockForMessage` with the waiter still registered in `link.waiters` and its `setTimeout` still live. The registry entry is then iterated by every live event on that channel until its own timer fires. The suite's own `withBlocking` helper asserts `parkedWaiters === 0` after every settled call and enumerates four exits (woken, timed out, aborted by disconnect, released by socket loss); the fifth — rejected — is not driven by any row.
failure: `fetchRecent({topic, since:'0', blockMs:5000})` with `conversations.history` starting to answer `ok:false, error:'internal_error'` 300ms into the block -> the call rejects with `SlackApiError: Slack conversations.history -> internal_error` and `link.waiters` still holds 1 waiter (measured directly in-process). It self-clears when the rung timer fires (<= MAX_DIAL_BACKOFF_MS = 5s), so this is a bounded leak, not an unbounded one.
remediation: Wrap the arm/re-query pair so the waiter is released on every exit, e.g. `try { const requeried = await this.runFetch({...args, since: floor}); ... } finally { wake(); }` — `wake()` is already idempotent (`if (done) return`) and self-deregistering, so calling it on the success path too is a no-op, and the subsequent `await wait` resolves immediately, which is the existing behaviour after a satisfied re-query.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a resource armed before an awaited call and released only on the returning exits. Add a REJECTION row to blocking-fetch.test.ts's degradation/exit tables — parameterize over the failure the re-query can hit (`internal_error` from conversations.history, `channel_not_found` -> NoSuchTopicError, a non-JSON 200 -> SlackShapeError) crossed with when it starts (before the first rung, mid-ladder, at the last rung), asserting both that the call rejects AND `parkedWaiters(plugin) === 0`. Route those rows through `withBlocking` so the existing registry assertion grades them; today it only ever sees calls that resolved.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `SocketModeLink.armWaiter`'s returned `wake`, whose body is `if (done) return; done = true; clearTimeout(timer); …; resolveWait();` — the `done` guard is what makes the extra call on the success path safe. Also relies on `await wait` resolving immediately once `resolveWait()` has already run, which it does because `wait` is a plain Promise resolved by that closure.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — the call still rejects with the same error; only the registry state at rejection changes.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I mutated armWaiter's registry cleanup away and watched blocking-fetch.test.ts go 51/53 red, which shows the parkedWaiters assertion is live and would go GREEN, not red, under this fix. The `wake()` call on the satisfied-re-query path at history.ts:178 becomes redundant but harmless; no test asserts wake is called exactly once.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is hidden: if the underlying transient failure remains, the caller still gets the same rejection and core still has to re-drive. It closes only the timer/registry residue. It does NOT address the adjacent question of whether a mid-ladder transient SHOULD abort the whole block rather than be retried on the next rung — that is a separate behavioural decision this fix deliberately does not make.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two callers blocked on one channel: caller A rejects and now calls wake() in its finally; A's wake only touches A's own `waiter` object and deletes the channel's Set only when it becomes empty, so B's waiter survives — verified against armWaiter's `set.delete(waiter); if (set.size === 0) this.waiters.delete(channel)`. Ordering A-then-B and B-then-A are symmetric. Interleaving with `stop()`: stop() drains via `waiter.wake()`, which sets `done`, so a later finally-wake is a no-op. Interleaving with the rung timer firing first: same `done` guard.

summary: `slack socket mode discipline > acks every pushed envelope, even while handlers are consuming events` asserts only `pushed ⊆ acked`, which is true whatever order the ack and the handler run in. Its comment claims the stronger property ("ack-first: acks precede handler processing, so none can be starved by a slow handler"), and that property is separately and much better graded by envelope-robustness.test.ts's `journalSends` rows, which patch `WebSocket.prototype.send` to capture CALL order and cross it with four handler behaviours including a 150ms event-loop block. The conformance copy is a strictly weaker restatement whose stated contract it cannot fail on.
failure: Mutation: moved the `ws.send(JSON.stringify({envelope_id}))` block in link.ts `onEnvelope` to AFTER `routeEnvelope`, so every ack now follows handler processing. Full slack suite: 4 failed, all four in envelope-robustness.test.ts `the ack precedes any handler processing`. conformance.test.ts's ack test passed. The test that claims ack-first in its own comment stayed green through the mutation that breaks ack-first.
remediation: Delete the `slack socket mode discipline` describe block from conformance.test.ts. The `pushed ⊆ acked` half is already subsumed by envelope-robustness.test.ts (which asserts it over DROPPED envelopes as well as surfaced ones) and the ordering half by its journal rows. summary: `pollUpdates` optional-chains `u?.message` and type-guards `typeof u?.update_id`, then two lines later dereferences `u.update_id` unguarded to build the diagnostic label. A `null` element in the `result` array throws a TypeError out of the for-loop, out of `pollUpdates`, and into connect's `.catch` — the ONE shared getUpdates consumer stops permanently while `post`/`fetchRecent` keep working, so the bridge looks connected and never ingests another message.
failure: Upstream (a middlebox, a proxy, or a non-conforming local Bot API server behind the documented `api_url` knob) answers `GET /getUpdates` with HTTP 200 `{"ok":true,"result":[null]}`. Reproduced: stderr shows exactly one line — `parley-telegram: getUpdates loop stopped: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'update_id')` — `fake.callCount('getUpdates')` stays at 1 forever, and after the upstream heals and a real message is injected, `fetchRecent` returns `[]`. Ingestion is dead for the life of the connection.
remediation: Screen the element before anything reads it: at the top of the `for (const u of updates)` body, `if (u === null || typeof u !== 'object') { diagnostics.report(`dropped a non-object update from getUpdates`, 'ingest'); continue; }`. The existing acknowledgement guard (`typeof u?.update_id === 'number' && Number.isSafeInteger(...)`) already refuses to advance `offset` past such an element, and the `MIN_IDLE_POLL_MS` floor already bounds the resulting re-poll — so a null element converges on the behaviour the package already blesses for a non-conforming `update_id`, instead of killing the loop.

The existing 'the ingestion loop survives $name from getUpdates' row set only varies the ENVELOPE, so no cell of it ever puts a hostile value inside a well-formed array; that is the hole this class lives in. Generalise the same generator to `sendMessage`'s result and to `getChat`'s.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: poll.ts's own acknowledgement guard, quoted: `if (typeof u?.update_id === 'number' && Number.isSafeInteger(u.update_id)) { offset = Math.max(offset, u.update_id + 1); }` — a null element fails it, so `offset` does not advance and the element stays in the backlog; and `if (offset === ackedBefore) { const idle = Date.now() - startedAt; if (idle < MIN_IDLE_POLL_MS) await delay(MIN_IDLE_POLL_MS - idle); }`, which bounds the re-poll to 4/s.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A getUpdates batch containing a null (or otherwise non-object) element: today a fatal TypeError that stops ingestion, after the fix a throttled stderr line with the loop alive and the batch's other updates still consumed.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I read envelope.test.ts ('the ingestion loop survives $name from getUpdates', 'keeps acknowledging updates when one arrives with no update_id'), poll-loop.test.ts (NON_CONFORMING_IDS, the error-status table, the watchdog rows) and ingest-faults.test.ts; none injects a non-object array element and none asserts the loop terminates.

summary: `journalText` writes `#served` only for ids that currently have records: `[...this.served].filter((id) => this.byChat.has(id))`. Every load-time repair and every compaction therefore silently drops the persisted protection for a chat a seam call named but that has not received a message yet — the one case the mark exists for, since `chat_map` chats are re-declared on every connect and seam-named chats are not. README's 'That protection is written into the store file, so a chat a seam call named in one run is still protected at the next load, before any seam call in the new process could have named it again' is false for that chat.
failure: Reproduced at the store level: `new ObservedStore(path, 1, 2)`; `serve('-700')` (a topic a `subscribe`/`fetchRecent` just named, no traffic yet) writes `#served ["-700"]`; 20 appends into chat `-1` drive a compaction; the file then contains no `#served` line at all. Next run: `-700`'s first real message is admitted, then two messages in fresh chats `-800`/`-801` displace it under `observed_max_chats: 2` — `store.entries('-700')` returns `[]`. The operator's own history is gone and the Bot API has no endpoint that can backfill it.
remediation: The filter is guarding the mark list against unbounded growth, and removing it outright unbounds the file across configuration changes (`this.served` is also re-read from the file each load, so it accumulates monotonically). Carry every id served IN THIS RUN plus every id that still holds records, and bound the union explicitly — e.g. cap the persisted list at the same order as `maxChats`, dropping the least-recently-served first — so an empty-but-named chat keeps its protection without the list growing forever.
testUpgrade: Add a RECORD-COUNT axis to `store.test.ts`'s SERVED_PERSISTENCE_CASES, which today appends a record for every served chat immediately after `serve()` and so can never see this. Parameterize each cell over `recordsPerServedChat ∈ [0, 1, 2]` and over `rewriteBefore ∈ ['none', 'compaction', 'load-repair']`, asserting after reload that `#served` still names the chat AND that a subsequent flood at the cap cannot evict it. Mirror it end-to-end in `docs.test.ts`'s 'keeps a chat a seam call named on load' by adding a cell whose seam call is a `fetchRecent` on a topic with no traffic, followed by enough flood traffic to force a compaction before the restart.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `ObservedStore.serve()`, quoted: `if (this.served.has(chatId)) return; this.served.add(chatId); this.file.note(...)` — the in-memory set is the source the persisted list must be derived from; and `admit()`'s `if (this.byChat.has(chatId) || this.served.has(chatId)) return true;`, which is what the mark buys.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A compaction now writes `#served` entries for chats holding zero retained records, so those chats are admitted past `observed_max_chats` and exempt from eviction in the next process before any seam call re-names them.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none

I checked store.test.ts SERVED_PERSISTENCE_CASES and CAP_CASES (both assert record contents and `size()`, not the mark list), IDENTITY_DAMAGE and LEGITIMATE_EVICTIONS (identity, not served marks), and rig.ts's `lineCount()` which filters out every `#`-prefixed line so line-count assertions are blind to it. The one to watch is unconfigured-chat-ingest.test.ts 'stays bounded under a flood of unknown chats', which counts ALL lines (`lines.length <= 2 * (2 * 4 + 2)`); it serves exactly one chat and that chat has records, so it is unaffected today, but a fix that grows the served list would show up there first.

summary: `StoreLock.replaceStale` opens `<store_path>.lock.break` with `wx` and returns false on any failure. A leftover `.lock.break` — what a SIGKILL between that create and the `finally` unlink leaves behind — therefore makes every future stale-claim take-over fail, forever, and nothing ever removes it. README's 'A claim naming a process that is gone is a crashed bridge's leftover and is replaced automatically' stops being true from then on.
failure: Reproduced: write `<path>.lock` containing the pid of an exited process, write `<path>.lock.break` containing the same dead pid, then `new StoreLock(path).claim()` throws `ObservedStore: '<path>' is already claimed by process 28905 through '<path>.lock' ...`. The bridge refuses to start after an ordinary crash. The message names `.lock` and removing it does work, so the state is recoverable — but only manually, and the orphan survives that removal, so every subsequent crash needs the same intervention.
remediation: On `wx` EEXIST for the break path, read its pid with the existing `lockHolder`, ask `processExists` (EPERM = alive, same as for `.lock`), and if it is dead unlink it and retry `wx` exactly once; give up as today if it is alive. Also name `.lock.break` in the claim error's recovery sentence so the manual path is complete.
testUpgrade: Parameterize `store-single-writer.test.ts`'s FOREIGN_CLAIMS over the SIBLING SET the store finds on disk, not just over the `.lock` contents: rows for `{lock: dead}`, `{lock: dead, break: dead}`, `{lock: dead, break: live}`, `{lock: live, break: dead}`, `{break: dead}` alone — each asserting whether the store opens and that exactly one holder ends up owning the file. Derive the sibling names from the suffix constants rather than hard-coding them, so a new sibling the store starts keeping gets a row automatically. The existing `store-lock-race.test.ts` sweep only drives a take-over from a clean starting state, so no cell of it can reach a pre-existing break file.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `processExists`, quoted: `try { process.kill(pid, 0); return true; } catch (err) { return (err as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code === 'EPERM'; }` — treating EPERM as alive is what stops a live-but-unsignallable take-over from being stolen; and `lockHolder`, which returns undefined for an unreadable file (an unreadable break file must therefore be treated as DEAD or the orphan case is unchanged).
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A store whose `.lock` names a dead pid and which carries a leftover `.lock.break` naming a dead (or unreadable) pid now opens automatically, as the README already promises.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — a `.lock.break` whose pid is alive still blocks the take-over, exactly as today.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. store-single-writer.test.ts's FOREIGN_CLAIMS never creates a `.lock.break`; store-lock-race.test.ts's 12-boundary sweep starts from a directory containing only `.lock`, and its invariant ('never two, and never none') is preserved by the fix.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied and the orphan is instead only reported rather than cleared, the bridge still refuses to start — the symptom moves from a misleading message to an accurate one, and automatic recovery stays broken. If the unlink is done WITHOUT the liveness re-check, two starters can each clear the other's in-flight take-over and both end up holding the store, which is the exact two-writers corruption the sibling exists to prevent.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two starters A and B both find a dead `.lock` and a dead-pid `.lock.break`. Both may reach the unlink; one ENOENTs (tolerated). Both then retry `wx` on the break path; exactly one wins, proceeds to `renameSync(break -> lock)`, and holds. The loser's `wx` gets EEXIST, returns false, and `claim()` throws — today's behaviour for a contended stale claim. If A holds a LIVE break file mid-take-over, B's `processExists` sees A alive, does not unlink, and fails as today. In no ordering do both hold.

summary: `readBounded` decodes the response bytes with `new TextDecoder()` and `buffered` hands the resulting STRING to `new Response(...)`, so the helper re-encodes every body as UTF-8. Any byte sequence that is not valid UTF-8 comes back replaced with U+FFFD, silently and with no error, and the copied `content-length` header no longer matches the body. The README calls the returned Response "already buffered" and says nothing about it being text-only.
failure: A server answering 200 with `application/octet-stream` body `89 50 4e 47 0d 0a 1a 0a ff d8 ff e0`: `await (await fetchWithRetry(url, {}, {label:'L', isStopped:()=>false})).arrayBuffer()` yields `ef bf bd 50 4e 47 0d 0a 1a 0a ef bf bd ef bf bd ef bf bd ef bf bd` — 22 bytes, four of the original bytes destroyed — while `res.headers.get('content-length')` still reports 12. Reproduced against a real node:http server in this worktree.
remediation: Keep the bytes: have `readBounded` return the joined `Uint8Array` alongside (or instead of) the decoded text, and build the replacement `Response` from the bytes — `new Response(size === 0 ? null : joined, { status, statusText, headers })`. Decode to a string only where one is needed (the error/redaction path). Either that, or state in the README and the `fetchWithRetry` JSDoc that the returned body is a UTF-8 text round-trip and is not byte-faithful, and drop `content-length` from the copied headers so the mismatch is not advertised.
testUpgrade: A parameterized round-trip case over BODY ENCODINGS rather than one payload: valid UTF-8 with astral characters, latin-1 high bytes, a lone 0x80 continuation byte, a PNG magic header, and an empty body — each asserted byte-for-byte via `Buffer.from(await res.arrayBuffer())` on the 2xx path and on an `allowStatuses` path, plus `content-length` agreeing with the body length. That guards the class (the buffering re-wrap changing what the caller is handed) rather than one binary payload, and would also catch a future truncation or header-copy regression; the existing error-envelope cases cannot, because every one of them serves ASCII 'A' repeated.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `errorBody(res, url)` in redact.ts — `return sanitizeBody(redactUrls(await res.text(), url));` — which still works over a byte-bodied Response, and `buffered`'s existing `const body = text.length === 0 ? null : text;` which becomes a size check so a 204/empty body still passes `null` to the Response constructor.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A binary or latin-1 body now reaches the caller byte-identically through `res.arrayBuffer()`.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I read every case in error-envelope.test.ts, fetch-with-retry-outcomes.test.ts and fetch-with-retry-redaction.test.ts; all of them serve ASCII, which is byte-identical either way, and the 204 case (`new Response(s === 204 ? null : 'body')`) reaches the empty branch through a size-0 check just as it does through a length-0 one. summary: `redactUrls` opens with `text.split(url).join('<url>')`. `''.split('')` splits a string into single characters, so an empty `url` interleaves `<url>` between every character of the untrusted body before it becomes an MCP `isError` result. The same file already guards exactly this hazard one level down — `credentialParts` filters shaped parts to `length > 1` and userinfo to `length > 0`, and the doc-comment there says an empty one "would split the body between every character" — but the top-level exact-URL split has no such guard.

The operator's diagnostic and the model's context are both destroyed, and a longer body would blow past MAX_ERROR_BODY as pure filler.

That guards the class (a redaction pass whose needle can be empty or degenerate) rather than the empty string, and it would also catch a future credential-part filter that let a 1-character needle back through.

remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: `redactUrls(text, '')` returns the text with only the scheme-anchored `URL_LIKE` sweep applied, instead of `<url>`-interleaved garbage.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none.

summary: 'Is this host loopback, and would a credential cross the wire in the clear' is one security invariant with FOUR implementations: packages/bridge-net-util/src/plaintext.ts `isLoopbackHost` (node:net isIPv4/isIPv6; used by discord/matrix/slack/telegram/zulip/redis); packages/bridge-nats/src/config.ts `plaintextRemoteServer` (hand-rolled authority split, reuses isLoopbackHost); packages/bridge-xmpp/src/config.ts `isPlaintextRemote` with its OWN `LOOPBACK_V4 = /^127(\.\d{1,3}){3}$/` plus a literal `host === '::1'`; and bridge-postgres's own default-credential path. Each carries its own tests — creds-warning.test.ts exists in 5 of 10 backends, in five different shapes — and the implementations disagree.
failure: Measured by importing all three classifiers into one probe over a 16-host corpus: 5 of 16 hosts are classified differently. `127.999.999.999` and `127.0.0.256` — not the loopback block; net-util and nats both warn — are classified LOOPBACK by xmpp's LOOPBACK_V4 (any four dot-separated 1-3 digit groups after 127), so `backend_config.service: 'xmpp://127.999.999.999:5222'` with a password sends SASL PLAIN with the cleartext-credential warning SILENCED, while the same host under redis or nats warns. In the other direction `0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1` and bare `::1` are loopback to net-util and remote to xmpp, and `[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]` is loopback to net-util and nats but remote to xmpp — three implementations, three answers for one address.

Scheme allowlists legitimately differ per protocol; host classification must not.

Put ONE shared host corpus in bridge-net-util (or bridge-core/src/testing, beside handle-corpus.ts and regex-corpus.ts) covering localhost / 127.x / octet-overflow / IPv6 short and long forms / bracketed / IPv4-mapped / integer-form / registrable lookalikes, and a parameterized test that runs EVERY exported plaintext classifier in the repo — discovered from the manifests, not hand-listed — over it and asserts they agree cell for cell.
